passages.title: The wise Book, a mercy for the good-doers
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are the opening of the surah, and they are best read in one breath rather than one at a time. A single movement runs through them: a Book is named, its effect is described, the people in whom that effect appears are portrayed, and a verdict is pronounced on them. Ibn Kathir reads them exactly this way — he quotes all five together and then comments on them as one continuous statement, ending with the words *"Whoever does this is one of those of whom Allah says: Such are on guidance from their Lord."* The passage is, in effect, a doorway with a description of the kind of person who walks through it.

## A Book, and the people it works on

The surah opens with الٓمٓ — *Alif Lam Mim*. Ibn Kathir does not re-explain these letters here. He simply notes that *"at the beginning of Surat Al-Baqarah we discussed the letters such as those that appear at the beginning of this Surah,"* and moves straight on. That restraint is itself instructive: he treats the matter as handled elsewhere and does not manufacture fresh meaning for it at each occurrence. His very next sentence goes to what Allah has *made* the Qur'an to be.

Then تِلۡكَ ءَايَٰتُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ ٱلۡحَكِيمِ — "These are the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom." Ibn Kathir's rendering is *"These are Ayat of the Wise Book."* The Book is not introduced as a set of instructions or a record of events; the first thing said about it is that it is wise.

The third ayah then tells us what this wise Book does, and for whom: هُدٗى وَرَحۡمَةٗ لِّلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ — "a guide and mercy for the good-doers." Ibn Kathir describes it more fully than the ayah's own two words: *"Allah has made the Qur'an a guidance and healing and a mercy for the Muhsinin."* He has added a third word — *healing* — alongside the guidance and mercy the ayah names. The Book does not merely inform; on his reading it also heals.

But everything here is attached to a named group: **al-muhsinin**, the *doers of ihsan*, the good-doers. Ibn Kathir defines them in a single clause, and both halves of it carry weight: they are *"those who do good deeds in accordance with the Shari'ah."* **Good deeds** — there must be real action, not sentiment. **In accordance with the Shari'ah** — the action must follow what Allah has legislated, rather than what a person decides is good on his own judgement.

Which raises the obvious question: what does such a life actually look like? The passage does not leave it abstract. It answers in the very next ayah.

## The portrait: prayer, zakah, certainty

ٱلَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَيُؤۡتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَهُم بِٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ هُمۡ يُوقِنُونَ — "those who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and have sure faith in the Hereafter."

Three marks: something between the servant and Allah, something between the servant and other people, and something inside the heart. Ibn Kathir fills in each one, and his expansion is worth taking slowly, because what he describes is not a bare minimum but the shape of a life.

**Prayer.** They *"establish the obligatory prayers in the proper manner and at the correct times, and follow that with regular, optional and supererogatory prayers."* Notice how much is packed into the word *establish* as Ibn Kathir reads it: the *how* (proper manner), the *when* (correct times), and then a further step — the obligatory prayers are the floor and not the ceiling, because the muhsin follows them with voluntary prayers on top. The person who only ever does the minimum is not yet the person this ayah is describing.

**Zakah.** They *"pay the Zakah to those who deserve it."* The qualification is part of the definition: zakah is not generosity in general but a due that reaches its rightful recipients. Ibn Kathir then adds a second item in the same breath: *"they uphold the ties of kinship with their relatives."* Wealth given and family kept appear together in his description of the same people.

**Certainty about the Hereafter.** They *"have certain faith that there will be rewards and punishments in the Hereafter, and they seek the reward with Allah."* This is not a vague hope that something comes after death. It is settled conviction about a reckoning — and, crucially, a decision about where to file the invoice.

Ibn Kathir draws that consequence out immediately: because they seek their reward with Allah, *"they do not show off or seek a reward or thanks from other people."* Certainty about the next world quietly reorganises this one. A person who is sure the account is kept there stops needing it settled here — stops needing to be seen praying, stops needing the recipient's gratitude, stops needing the relative to acknowledge the visit. Showing off is, at bottom, a bill presented to the wrong payer.

## Zakah in Makkah — a point of real substance

The words يُؤۡتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ, "they pay Zakah," raise a historical question, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼan takes it up: this is a Makkan verse, yet it carries the injunction of zakah. The conclusion drawn is that *"the original injunction of Zakah had already been revealed before Hijrah, right there in Makkah al-Muʿazzamah."*

What, then, of the widely held view that zakah was made obligatory in the second year after the Hijrah? Maʿārif ul Qurʼan answers that this refers to something more specific: *"the arrangement of fixing its nisab (threshold), providing details of obligatory amount to be paid, collecting and disbursing it on authorized heads by the Islamic government."* That administrative framework — the threshold at which zakah becomes due, the exact amounts, the state collection and distribution — was indeed put in place in the second year of Hijrah. The duty itself was older.

The commentary strengthens the case with a second witness. Ibn Kathir, commenting on وَأَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُوا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ ("Establish Salah and pay Zakah," 73:20), *"has arrived at the same conclusion,"* since Surah Al-Muzzammil is a Makkan surah revealed *"during the very initial period of the revelation of the Qur'an"* — and it already commands zakah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼan then draws the lesson out: *"the way Salah and Zakah have been described mostly side by side in the verses of the Qur'an, its obligation had also taken effect side by side."* The pairing you meet all through the Qur'an is not a stylistic habit; on this reading the two duties entered the life of the believing community together. Our ayah preserves exactly that pairing. And the commentary closes the discussion as scholars do with historical judgements: *Allah knows best.*

## The verdict

أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ عَلَىٰ هُدٗى مِّن رَّبِّهِمۡۖ وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ — "It is they who are truly guided by their Lord, and it is they who are the successful."

The word *hudan*, guidance, has already appeared in ayah 3, where the Book is guidance for such people; here in ayah 5 such people are said to be upon guidance from their Lord. The passage closes its own circle.

Ibn Kathir's gloss on "Such are on guidance from their Lord" is brief and pointed: it means *"they follow His guidance with clear understanding."* Not stumbling along by habit or inheritance — following with their eyes open, knowing what they are doing and why.

Then the last word: **al-muflihun**, the successful. Ibn Kathir's comment is short and expansive at once — successful *"in this world and in the Hereafter."* Not a consolation prize deferred to the next life while this one is written off. The good-doer's life works, here as well as there.

## Living it

Read as a whole, the passage says something to anyone who picks up the Qur'an: its guidance, healing and mercy are not automatic. The pages are the same for everyone; the effect is not. What makes the difference, on Ibn Kathir's reading, is whether a person brings to the Book good deeds done in accordance with what Allah has legislated.

Ayah 4 turns that into a checklist, and it is deliberately ordinary:

- **Pray the obligatory prayers properly and at their times** — and then, once that is steady, add the voluntary prayers on top, as Ibn Kathir describes.
- **Give the zakah to those who deserve it**, and keep up the ties of kinship with relatives — the two things he names side by side.
- **Ask who you are performing for.** If other people's recognition is what would complete the deed for you, this ayah has something to say: those who are certain of the Hereafter seek their reward with Allah, and do not show off or look to people for thanks.

And if that sounds like a high bar, ayah 5 is the encouragement. Those who live this way are not merely trying. They are, in Allah's own words, upon guidance from their Lord — and they are the successful, in this world and in the Hereafter.

passages.title: Buyers of idle talk versus heirs of the Gardens
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat set two kinds of people side by side and let the contrast do the teaching: a man who spends his wealth and attention on "idle talk" to pull people away from Allah's path, and the believers who believe and do righteous deeds and are given Gardens of Delight forever. Holding the passage together is a single question — **what did you buy with your life, and what did you get for it?**

## The setting: a merchant, a stack of Persian stories, and a plan

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the occasion of revelation. The verse came down because of an event relating to **Naḍr ibn Ḥārith**, one of the top businessmen among the idolaters (*mushriks*) of Makkah. On one journey he bought and brought back from Iran a collection of historical stories featuring Cyrus and other Persian kings, and said to the Quraysh of Makkah: *Muhammad tells you the stories of the people of ʿĀd and Thamūd and others — I shall tell you better stories, those of Rustam, Isfandyār and other kings of Persia.*

They listened eagerly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts a finger on why: his stories "contained no lessons to learn and no work to do." Many of the idolaters had some measure of interest in the Divine Word because of its miraculous nature — they used to listen to it stealthily — and Naḍr's entertainment handed them an excuse to draw away from the Qur'an.

A narration from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) in *Ad-Durr al-Manthūr* sharpens the picture. The same merchant had brought in a singing bondwoman he had bought in a foreign country, and through her devised a plan to stop people from listening to the Qur'an: whenever he found someone intending to go and listen, he would have him hear her sing first. He used to say: *Muhammad makes you listen to the Qur'an, then goes on to ask you to pray and fast, which make life difficult for you. Come, listen to this and enjoy the fun.*

So the "idle talk" of ayah 6 was, in its first instance, either those tales of the Persian kings or that singing bondwoman — in both cases a campaign against revelation. That is why the verse adds **li-yuḍilla ʿan sabīl Allāh**, "to mislead from the path of Allah" — which Ibn Kathir explains as meaning *he does this to oppose Islam and its followers*. This was not a man drifting into distraction; it was a man engineering distraction for others.

## "He purchases" — the word that carries the ayah

The verb is **yashtarī**, from *ishtirāʾ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it literally means "to buy," and in the story of Naḍr it is used in the real sense — he actually paid money for the tales and for the singer. But on occasions the same word carries a second sense in the Qur'an: **doing one act instead of another**, as in *"those who have bought error at the price of guidance"* (2:16, and again 2:175). Read that way — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the word here also carries this general sense — the ayah reaches anyone who takes amusement *in place of* revelation, whether or not a coin changes hands.

Qatādah, quoted by Ibn Kathir, makes precisely this point: *"By Allah, he may not spend money on it, but his purchasing it means he likes it, and the more misguided he is, the more he likes it and the more he prefers falsehood to the truth and harmful things over beneficial things."* **Your affections are your currency.**

## "Lahw al-ḥadīth" — idle talk, and what counts as it

The phrase Allah uses is **lahw al-ḥadīth**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens both words:

- **Ḥadīth** here is used in the sense of tales told and things said and done.
- **Lahw** literally means *to become heedless*. So it covers things that make a person negligent of what must be done, and also things that bring no worthwhile benefit but serve merely as pastime or entertainment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the sayings of the commentators differ here:

**The narrower reading.** In a narration of Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir (may Allah be pleased with them) it is explained as music, vocal or instrumental — reported and verified, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, by al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqī in *ash-Shuʿab*. Ibn Kathir preserves Ibn Masʿūd's emphatic comment on this very ayah: *"This — by Allah — refers to singing."* Ibn Kathir also mentions the view that "purchases idle talk" means buying singing servant girls.

**The broader reading.** In the view of the majority of the Companions, the Successors (*Tābiʿīn*) and the commentators at large, *lahw al-ḥadīth* applies generally to **everything which makes one fall into a state of heedlessness as to the remembrance and worship of Allah** — including music accompanied by instruments, and obscene or absurd fictional narratives. Ibn Jarīr took this general sense: all speech that hinders people from seeing the signs of Allah and following His path. Imām al-Bukhārī in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* and al-Bayhaqī in his *Sunan* both elected to go by this reading.

The two readings are not rivals: as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, even those who read the phrase generally include singing and instrumental music within it — the difference is one of scope, not of exclusion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a narration of **Tirmidhi** in which the Prophet ﷺ said, *"Do not buy or sell singing bondwomen,"* and then said that it was about such things that this verse was revealed — adduced as further proof of the phrase's general sense.

## "And takes it in mockery": the last step

Ayah 6 adds **wa yattakhidhahā huzuwā** — "and takes it by way of mockery." Mujāhid, quoted by Ibn Kathir, explains: *this means mocking the path of Allah and making fun of it.*

The recompense fits exactly. **ʿAdhāb muhīn** — a *humiliating* torment. Ibn Kathir draws out the correspondence: just as they showed no respect to the signs and path of Allah, so they will be shown no respect on the Day of Resurrection, and they will be subjected to a painful, ongoing torment.

## Ayah 7: the body language of rejection

Ayah 7 films the man in the moment of refusal: *"And when Our verses are recited to such a one, he turns away in pride, as if he heard them not — as if there were deafness in his ear."* Ibn Kathir explains that when these Qur'anic verses are recited to one who is fond of idleness and play, he turns away from them and does not want to hear them, **because it annoys him to hear them**.

Allah does not say the man *is* deaf. He says he turns away **in pride** — *mustakbiran* — *as if* he had not heard it. His ears work; the turning away is the act of a proud man who finds the words irritating.

Then comes **fa-bashshirhu bi-ʿadhābin alīm** — "so announce to him a painful torment." Ibn Kathir notes the precision of the exchange: that torment on the Day of Resurrection will hurt him just as much as listening to the Book of Allah and its verses hurt him.

Ibn Kathir sets this scene against its opposite, first mentioning the blessed who benefit from hearing the Book of Allah: *"Allah has sent down the Best Statement, a Book, its parts resembling each other and oft-repeated. The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it. Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah"* (39:23). He connects that with the doomed, who turn away from the Qur'an and do not benefit from the Words of Allah, turning instead to flutes and singing accompanied by musical instruments. As Ibn Kathir also cites, *"Say: It is for those who believe a guide and a healing. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness (deafness) in their ears, and it is blindness for them"* (41:44), and *"We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy to those who believe, and it increases the wrongdoers in nothing but loss"* (17:82).

## Ayat 8–9: the other purchase

Against all of that, ayah 8 turns: *"Verily, those who believe and do righteous good deeds, for them are Gardens of Delight."*

Ibn Kathir explains that here Allah mentions the destiny of the righteous in the Hereafter — those who believe in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and do righteous deeds in accordance with the Laws of Allah. And *Jannāt an-naʿīm*, "Gardens of Delight," means that there they will enjoy all kinds of delights and pleasures: food, drink, clothing, dwelling-places, means of transportation, women, a light of beauty and delightful sounds — things which have never crossed the mind of any human being.

Ayah 9 secures it with three seals:

1. **Khālidīna fīhā** — abiding there. Ibn Kathir adds a beautiful gloss: they will stay there forever, *never leaving and never desiring change*.
2. **Waʿda Allāhi ḥaqqā** — "a promise of Allah in truth." Ibn Kathir: this will undoubtedly come to pass, for it is a promise from Allah, and Allah never breaks His promise, because He is the Most Generous Bestower who does what He wills and is able to do all things.
3. **Wa huwa al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm.** Ibn Kathir explains *al-ʿAzīz*, the All-Mighty, as the One who has subjugated all things and to whom all things submit; and *al-Ḥakīm*, the All-Wise, in what He says and what He does, the One who has made this Qur'an a guidance to the believers.

## Living it: what the passage actually asks

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the legal implications, and its most important move is to distinguish degrees rather than issue a blanket verdict. Its starting observation is that wherever the Qur'an mentions *lahw* and *laʿib* (play and game), it is in the context of disparagement — the lowest degree of which is *karāhah* (reprehensibility).

**First, the offence here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that playing which becomes a conduit of going astray from one's religion, or of making others turn away from it, is *kufr* (infidelity) — and that in ayah 6 it has been declared an act of grave error and infidelity, the punishment of which is painful, a punishment particular to those who have disbelieved. That is the top of the scale, not the everyday case.

**Second, the middle case:** that which does not make people go astray from Islamic beliefs, but does involve them in something forbidden and sinful. This would not be *kufr*, but it remains patently unlawful and gravely sinful — as with all games played with bets, where the element of gambling (*qimār*) is present with money given or taken on winning and losing, or recreational activities that impede prayers, fasting and other duties. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places here the reading of shameless fiction and indecent poetry, and the study by common people of the ideas of the wayward proponents of falsehood — while noting that if scholars well grounded in religious knowledge study such material in order to refute it, it does not matter.

**Third, the ordinary case:** games with neither an element of *kufr* nor of open sinfulness are *makrūh* (reprehensible), in that one wastes his energy and time in an activity that yields no benefit.

**And what is not "lahw" at all.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a report of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) in the *Kitāb al-Jihād* of **al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak** that the Prophet ﷺ said: every *lahw* of the world is false except three — that you play with your bow and arrow, that you play while training your horse, and that you play with your wife — "because these are among acceptable rights." (On its chain: al-Ḥākim said it is sahih on the condition set forth by Muslim, while adh-Dhahabī and others did not accept it as *muttaṣil* (of an uninterrupted chain) but called it *mursal* — though in the sight of the majority of hadith experts a *mursal* hadith is also authentic.) A parallel narration from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir (may Allah be pleased with him), in **Abū Dāwūd, Tirmidhi, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah**, puts it even more precisely: *three things do not fall under lahw* — a man training his horse, playing with his wife, and shooting with his bow and arrows.

As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, these are not exceptions carved out of a prohibition; they are simply not included under the definition of *lahw*, because *lahw* is supposed to be something in which there is no worthwhile religious or worldly benefit, and these three are worthwhile — archery and the training of horses being part of the preparation for jihad, and playfulness with one's wife serving the purpose of procreation. By the same logic, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rates as allowed by the Sharīʿah those games played to maintain physical health and mobility, or for some other religious or worldly need, or at least for relief from fatigue without excessive indulgence that disrupts necessary duties — and if undertaken with the intention of fulfilling a religious need, they are *thawāb*-worthy (rewardable) as well.

The sources give warm illustrations. Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ (may Allah be pleased with him) sought and received the Prophet's ﷺ permission to race a man of the Anṣār whom no one could beat — which, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, tells us foot racing is permissible. When the well-known wrestler Rukānah challenged the Prophet ﷺ, he accepted the challenge and won the bout (Abū Dāwūd in *al-Marāsīl*). Some Ethiopian young men used to play with spears as a rehearsal, and the Prophet ﷺ let Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) watch their game of martial skill while she stood behind his back, saying to the performers, *"Have fun, keep playing"* — and in some narrations, *"I do not like that people see harshness in your religion"* (reported by al-Bayhaqī in *ash-Shuʿab*, as in *al-Kanz*). And a report transmitted by Abū Dāwūd in his *Marāsīl* from Ibn Shihāb — attributed to the Prophet ﷺ *mursalan* — says: *"Let your hearts rest now and then."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this as proof that recreation meant to relax the mind and heart is permissible.

The condition throughout, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is that the correct and sound objective of these activities stays in view. **Playing for the sake of playing should never be the objective**, and even legitimate recreation is restricted to the measure of need; any indulgence stretching to unreasonable proportions would not be in order.

**On music specifically**, the sources are strict. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Imām Abū Ḥanīfah, Mujāhid, Muhammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah and others explained *az-zūr* ("falsehood") in *"those who do not witness falsehood"* (25:72) as *ghinā* — singing and the playing of instrumental music. It cites **Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah in their Sunans and Ibn Ḥibbān in his Sahih**, from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said some people of his community would drink wine giving it a name other than its own, with instruments and singing women in attendance, and that Allah would make the earth sink with them. And from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), reported by **Imām Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Ḥibbān**, that Allah has forbidden wine, gambling, the drum and the *sārangī* (a stringed instrument), and that everything that intoxicates is unlawful.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites a long narration from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), reported by **Tirmidhi** and called by him *hasan gharīb*, listing conditions after which grave punishment and the signs of the Hour may be expected — among them zakāh taken as a penalty, religious learning acquired for worldly objectives, wicked people respected out of fear of them, singing girls and musical instruments appearing all over, and wines of all sorts consumed — after which one may await a red storm, an earthquake, the sinking of the earth, and the signs following one another like a broken necklace with its beads scattered. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's comment is that this is an advance warning: Muslims must remain vigilant and take precautions against these sins, personally and socially, before they become accepted common practice.

Where narrations appear to point the other way, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconciles them thus: what is forbidden is the singing of a non-*mahram* woman, and song accompanied by musical instruments; but if poetic compositions are recited in a pleasing voice, and the reciter is not a woman or a beardless young man, and the subject matter is not vulgar or indecent and does not include any other sin, then it is permissible. The *samāʿ* attributed to some revered Sufis is understood as this permissible kind, since it is certain that they followed the Sharīʿah and Sunnah faithfully.

## The one thing to carry away

Every one of us is *yashtarī* — buying — all day long, with hours and attention rather than dirhams. The passage does not condemn rest or enjoyment: the Prophet ﷺ told those young men with their spears to have fun and keep playing. What ayah 6 exposes is the trade in which a person hands over his receptivity to Allah's words and takes amusement in exchange, until — as ayah 7 shows — revelation itself becomes the thing that annoys him to hear. Ayat 8 and 9 seal the other side of the ledger with *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm*: believe, act on it, and the promise is a promise of Allah in truth, in Gardens they will never leave and never desire to change.

passages.title: Pillarless heavens and the challenge to false gods
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are a single argument for Allah's oneness, built out of things the listener can see with his own eyes. Ayah 10 walks the eye from the sky down to the mountains, across the animals, and into the growing earth; ayah 11 then turns and asks the idolater a question he cannot answer: you have just seen what Allah made — now show Me one thing your gods made.

Ibn Kathir sets the theme at the outset: here "Allah explains His mighty power in creating the heavens and the earth, and everything that is within them and between them."

## The roof with no pillars

The passage opens: **"He has created the heavens without any pillars that you see"** (ayah 10).

The Arabic is خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ بِغَيۡرِ عَمَدٖ تَرَوۡنَهَا — *khalaqa's-samāwāti bi-ghayri ʿamadin tarawnahā*. *ʿAmad* is the word rendered "pillars"; *tarawnahā* is the word rendered "you see." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the same statement appears earlier in Sūrah ar-Raʿd — **"Allah is the One who raised the heavens without pillars. You see them"** (13:2) — rendered there with a different translation, and observes that, analysed grammatically, the text admits two alternative meanings.

**Where the ambiguity lies.** The word *tarawnahā* carries a pronoun ("them"), and that pronoun can attach to two different things. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the options out:

1. **The pronoun refers back to *ʿamad*, the pillars.** Then the phrase is describing the pillars: pillars *of the kind you may see*. The sense becomes: Allah created the skies without pillars that you may see — that is, had the pillars been there, you would have seen them. When pillars are not seen, it is clear that this great roof of the sky has been erected without pillars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this explanation, via Ibn Kathir, from **Sayyidnā Ḥasan and Qatādah**. Ibn Kathir gives their words directly: *"It does not have any pillars, visible or invisible."*

2. **The pronoun refers back to *as-samāwāt*, the skies themselves**, with the sentence standing independently. Then the meaning is: Allah created the skies without pillars, as you see. Your own eyes are the witness.

3. **A further possibility within the first analysis:** that the phrase concedes pillars but denies their visibility — *the skies stand on pillars you cannot see; they are invisible.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this last explanation, again via Ibn Kathir, from **Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid** (may Allah be pleased with them).

This is a place where the early authorities genuinely differed, and the sources set the views side by side rather than settling the matter. Notice what the disagreement is *not* about. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point plainly: **"No matter what the option, the verse does point out to the particular sign of the perfect power of Allah Taʿālā that He has made this extensive, high and magnificent roof in a way that no column and pillar is seen there-under."** Whether there is nothing at all beneath the sky, or something beneath it that no eye can reach, the sign is the same — you look up at the largest structure you will ever see, and there is nothing under it that you can see.

That is the argument's first move, and it is deliberately made with the reader's head tilted back. It does not ask you to accept a report. It asks you to look.

## Down to the earth: mountains, creatures, rain

From the sky, ayah 10 brings the eye down: **"and has set on the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you."**

The word rendered "firm mountains" is *rawāsiya*. Ibn Kathir explains these as "the mountains which stabilize and lend weight to the earth, lest it should shake with its water." The Qur'an's own phrase for the purpose is **أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ** — *an tamīda bikum*, "lest it should shake **with you**," and Ibn Kathir pauses on exactly that phrase. The mountains are not described in the abstract; the wording puts *you*, the human being standing on the surface, inside the sentence.

Then: **"And He has scattered therein moving creatures of all kinds."** Ibn Kathir: "He has placed throughout it all kinds of animals, the total number of whose kinds and colors is known to no one except the One Who created them." That is a quiet but devastating point in an argument about false gods. The catalogue of what has been made exceeds the knowledge of every creature; only the Maker knows the full inventory of His own making.

Then the sequence turns from creation to provision: **"And We send down water from the sky, and We cause (plants) of every goodly kind to grow therein in pairs."** Ibn Kathir draws out the logic of the ordering: *"When Allah tells us that He is the Creator, He also reminds us that He is the Provider."* The One who raised the roof is the One who sends the rain through it. Making and sustaining are not two departments; they belong to one Lord.

On **"every goodly kind... in pairs"**, Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as "every kind of good produce in pairs, i.e., they are beautiful to look at."

Ibn Kathir then records a striking remark from **ash-Shaʿbī**: *"People are also produce of the earth, so whoever enters Paradise is goodly and whoever enters Hell is vile."* The image reaches further than botany. If human beings too are what the earth brings forth, then the same word that sorts good crops from bad sorts human lives — and the harvest is Paradise or the Fire. A verse about rain and plants has, in one sentence, become a verse about you.

## "Now show Me"

Ayah 11 gathers all of it into one phrase: **هَٰذَا خَلۡقُ ٱللَّهِ** — *hādhā khalqu'llāh*, "This is the creation of Allah."

"This" gathers up everything just listed. Ibn Kathir spells out the reference: it means "all that Allah has mentioned here of the creation of the heavens and earth and everything in between stems from His power of creation and control alone, and He has no partner or associate in that."

Then the challenge: **فَأَرُونِي مَاذَا خَلَقَ ٱلَّذِينَ مِن دُونِهِۦ** — *fa-arūnī mādhā khalaqa'lladhīna min dūnih*, "So, show Me that which those besides Him have created." Ibn Kathir identifies who is meant: "those idols and rivals whom you worship and call upon."

Feel the shape of the demand. It is not *tell Me* but **show Me**. The passage opened by inviting the eye to look at Allah's work, and it closes by inviting the eye to look at anyone else's. The witness is the same in both cases: your own sight. Allah's making is spread across the sky and the earth and every living thing on it, visible to anyone who lifts his head. The rival gods are asked for one item — anything at all — and the hands come back empty.

Note also who is speaking. "Show **Me**" — the challenge is issued by Allah Himself in the first person. This is not a debater's flourish; it is the Creator putting the claim of every rival to the test in front of the one who worships it.

## "Nay, the wrongdoers are in plain error"

Since no answer comes, the verse supplies the verdict: **بَلِ ٱلظَّـٰلِمُونَ فِى ضَلَـٰلٍ مُّبِينٍ**.

Ibn Kathir takes it clause by clause:

- **"Nay, the wrongdoers"** — *aẓ-ẓālimūn* — "means the idolators who associate others in worship with Allah." That is worth sitting with. The Qur'an's word for the person who sets up partners with Allah in worship is *ẓālim*, wrongdoer — not merely someone who has reasoned badly, but someone who has committed an injustice, giving to another what belongs only to the One who made it all.
- **"in error"** — *fī ḍalāl* — "means, they are ignorant and blind."
- **"plain"** — *mubīn* — "means, it is clear and obvious, and not at all hidden."

That final word closes the circuit of the passage. The whole argument has turned on what is *visible*: no pillars seen under the sky, mountains set on the earth to steady it, animals scattered across it, crops beautiful to look at. And the error itself is *mubīn* — equally out in the open, nothing hidden about it. A person surrounded on every side by the evidence of one Maker, still calling on things that have made nothing.

## Living it

**Let creation actually argue with you.** The passage does not reason from abstractions. It reasons from the sky, the mountains, the animals, the rain, the crops — ordinary sights the listener saw every day and stopped noticing. The remedy these ayat prescribe for heedlessness is simply to look properly. Look up once and register that nothing is holding it up that you can see. That is the exercise ayah 10 is setting.

**Hold Creator and Provider together.** Ibn Kathir's observation — that when Allah tells us He is the Creator, He also reminds us that He is the Provider — is a comfort as well as a proof. The same power that raised the heavens sends down the water that feeds you. Trusting one and worrying about the other does not make sense.

**Apply "show Me" honestly.** The challenge of ayah 11 was framed against the idols and rivals people worshipped and called upon, but its logic is a question anyone can put to whatever he leans on: *what has it made?* Whatever a person hangs his hope, fear, and obedience on has, at the end of the accounting, created nothing.

**Take *ẓālim* seriously.** Ibn Kathir's gloss ties the word for wrongdoing directly to associating others with Allah in worship. And ash-Shaʿbī's remark warns where the sorting ends up: people, like produce, come up goodly or vile, and the harvest is Paradise or the Fire. The passage is not only teaching us about the sky. It is asking which kind of growth we are.

passages.title: Luqman's wisdom: gratitude, shirk, and parents
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat introduce Luqman — a man Allah gave wisdom to, though the majority of scholars held he was not a prophet — and then open his counsel to his son. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the order: of all the wise advice Luqman gave, what comes first is soundness of belief. Ayah 12 commands Luqman to be grateful to Allah; ayah 13 warns his son against shirk; ayat 14–15 command kindness and gratitude to parents, and then set the one boundary that even a parent's demand cannot cross.

## Who was Luqman?

The Salaf differed over him, and the difference is worth knowing because of what it says about honour in Allah's sight.

**Prophet or righteous servant?** Ibn Kathir reports two opinions among the Salaf: that he was a prophet, or that he was a righteous servant of Allah without prophethood. **The majority favoured the second**. Mujahid said plainly, "Luqman was a righteous servant, but he was not a Prophet." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the report making him a prophet comes only from ʿIkrimah, and the authority of that report is weak; Imam al-Baghawi reports a consensus that he was a man of wisdom, knowledgeable in religious law, but not a prophet.

This matters for reading ayah 12. If Luqman was not a prophet, how was he "told" to be grateful? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the command could have been given to him through *ilhām* — inspiration, of the kind attributed to the friends of Allah (*awliyāʾ Allāh*).

**Who he was in the world.** Sufyan ath-Thawri narrated from al-Ashʿath, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Luqman was an Ethiopian slave who was a carpenter." ʿAbdullah bin az-Zubayr asked Jabir bin ʿAbdullah what he had heard about Luqman, and Jabir said he was short with a flat nose, and came from Nubia. Saʿid bin al-Musayyib said he was from the black peoples of southern Egypt, with thick lips — "Allah gave him wisdom but withheld prophethood from him." Mujahid described him as a thick-lipped, cracked-footed Ethiopian slave.

Ibn Kathir preserves a scene that should be read slowly. Al-Awzaʿi relates from ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Harmalah that a black man came to Saʿid bin al-Musayyib with a question, and Saʿid said to him: do not be upset because you are black, for among the best of people were three who were black — Bilal, Mahjaʿ the freed slave of ʿUmar bin al-Khattab, and Luqman the Wise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the same incident, adding that Saʿid — the famous Tabiʿi — was consoling the man about the colour of his skin by naming three of the most revered people anywhere.

**The tongue and the heart.** Ibn Jarir records from Khalid ar-Rabaʿi that Luqman's master told him to slaughter a sheep and bring the best two pieces of it; he brought the tongue and the heart. Later the master said, bring the worst two morsels; he brought the tongue and the heart. When the master objected, Luqman said: there is nothing better than these two if they are good, and nothing worse than these two if they are bad.

**The secret of his standing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that while Luqman was addressing a large gathering, a man asked him bluntly: aren't you the one who used to graze goats with me in such-and-such a forest? Luqman said yes. The man asked how he had come to a station where crowds travelled from far and wide to hear him. Luqman answered that it came from two things: always telling the truth, and avoiding useless things. Another report gives a fuller list, which he offered as the path to the same rank: lower your gaze and hold your tongue; stay content with lawful sustenance; guard your private parts; tell the truth and uphold it; fulfil the pledge; honour the guest; protect the neighbour; observe silence against wasteful speech and leave off useless indulgences.

Other reports fill in his life: Wahb ibn Munabbih said he was a nephew of Ayyub (peace be upon him), while Muqatil identified him as his brother through his maternal aunt; Tafsīr al-Baiḍāwī and other sources say he lived long, into the time of Dawud (peace be upon him). Before Dawud received prophethood Luqman used to give people rulings, and he stopped once Dawud was raised, believing he was no longer needed. Some reports say he was a judge among the Bani Israʾil. Wahb ibn Munabbih said he had read more than ten thousand of Luqman's words of wisdom (Qurtubi).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes that Ibn Kathir pointed to an unusual report from Qatadah that Luqman was given a choice between prophethood and wisdom, and chose wisdom. Asked why, he is reported to have said: the office of a prophet carries great responsibilities; had it been given to me without my choosing it, Allah would have been sufficient to enable me to discharge it as due — but if I had asked for it by my own choice, the responsibility would have been mine. Because the source itself flags this as an unusual report, hold it lightly.

## "We gave Luqman wisdom" — what is ḥikmah?

Ibn Kathir glosses *al-ḥikmah* in ayah 12 as **understanding, knowledge and eloquence**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the word occurs in the Qur'an twenty times carrying several senses — wisdom, knowledge, reason, forbearance, patience, prophethood, and correctness of opinion.

Abu Hayyan defined it as "a statement in words, a statement that teaches people a lesson, a lesson that goes down their hearts and which they conserve and communicate to others" — wisdom that travels, which is precisely what happened to Luqman's advice. Ibn ʿAbbas said ḥikmah is intellect, understanding and intelligence; others said it is acting in accordance with knowledge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says there is no real contradiction — all of it falls under ḥikmah — and cites Mawlana Ashraf ʿAli Thanawi's rendering of it as prudence and wisdom, explained as **knowledge that has been put into practice**. That is the useful test: wisdom is not merely what you know, but what your knowledge has become in your conduct.

## Ayah 12: gratitude that only benefits you

The command to Luqman is "Give thanks to Allah." Ibn Kathir explains it as a command to give thanks for the blessings and favours Allah had given him alone among his people and contemporaries.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two ways of reading the grammar. The first supplies an understood "We said": We gave Luqman ḥikmah and commanded him to be grateful. On the second, the phrase *ani-shkur lillāh* is itself the **explanation of what the ḥikmah was** — the wisdom given to Luqman was that Allah commanded him to be grateful and he carried it out. On that reading, **being grateful for the blessings of Allah is the greatest wisdom there is.**

Then the ayah turns to us. "And whoever gives thanks, he gives thanks for the good of himself." Ibn Kathir: the benefit of that comes back to him, and Allah's reward is for those who give thanks — as Allah says elsewhere, "and whosoever does righteous good deeds, then such will prepare a good place for themselves" (30:44). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that according to the law of Allah, whoever is grateful to Him, He causes an increase in the blessings given to that person.

"And whoever is unthankful, then verily, Allah is Rich, Worthy of all praise." Ibn Kathir: He has no need of His servants and will not be harmed by their ingratitude — **even if all the people of the earth were to disbelieve** — for He has no need of anything or anyone besides Himself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same point about the command itself: it was not given so that Allah might gain some benefit from it. He needs gratefulness from no one; the command was given in the interest of human beings and for their own benefit. Worship, in other words, is not a favour we do for Allah. Ibn Kathir ends there with the creed itself: there is no god but He, and we worship none but Him.

## Ayah 13: the greatest wrong of all

Ibn Kathir gives Luqman's full name as Luqman bin ʿAnqaʾ bin Sadun, and his son's name as Tharan, on a saying quoted by as-Suhayli. Then he makes the point that gives ayah 13 its force: Luqman was advising **the closest and most beloved of all people to him**, the one who deserved to be given the best of his knowledge. And the best thing he had to give was: worship Allah alone, and associate nothing with Him.

The word the ayah uses is *ẓulm*, which the sources render as wrong, injustice, or grave transgression. Ibn Kathir glosses "indeed shirk is a great ẓulm" as meaning **it is the greatest wrong**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the logic plainly: one should take nothing other than Allah as an object of worship, for no injustice in this world can be as grave as that of a person who stoops to equate some creation of Allah with the Creator.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites al-Bukhari, recording from ʿAbdullah, that when the ayah "It is those who believe and confuse not their belief with ẓulm" (6:82) was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were distressed and said: who among us does not confuse his belief with ẓulm? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is not what it means. Have you not heard what Luqman said: 'O my son! Join not in worship others with Allah. Verily, joining others in worship with Allah is a great ẓulm indeed'?" Ibn Kathir notes it was recorded by Muslim as well.

So the Prophet ﷺ himself used ayah 13 to explain 6:82. The ẓulm that ayah warns of is shirk. That is at once a mercy for the anxious believer and a warning about where the real danger lies.

## Ayat 14–15: the interjection about parents

Notice the shift in voice. Ayah 13 is Luqman speaking; ayah 14 is **Allah speaking** — "And We have enjoined on man…". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the placement: more of Luqman's counsel to his son follows later, and in between this command appears in order to highlight the gravity of shirk — that it must be avoided under all circumstances, including the most emotionally costly one imaginable.

Ibn Kathir points out that worshipping Allah alone and honouring parents are **often mentioned together** in the Qur'an, as in "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him. And that you be dutiful to your parents" (17:23).

**"His mother bore him, wahnan ʿalā wahn."** The Arabic doubles the word for weakness and stacks it on itself. The early authorities each caught a different facet: Mujahid said it means the hardship of bearing the child; Qatadah said "exhaustion upon exhaustion"; ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani said "weakness upon weakness." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: she kept the child in her body for nine months, vigilant and protective the whole time, her weakness and discomfort increasing day by day — and then even after the birth came the feeding, a task demanding painstaking attention day and night, which added further to her already receding strength.

Ibn Kathir says Allah mentions how the mother brings the child up, how she grows tired and suffers stress from staying up with the child night and day, **to remind the son of her previous kind treatment of him** — and connects it to the du'a of 17:24: "My Lord! Bestow on them Your mercy as they did bring me up when I was young."

Because it is the mother who faces most of the hardship in bringing up the child, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, **the right of the mother has been made to precede even the right of the father** in the Shariʿah of Islam; and it says this is exactly what the wording of ayah 14 comes to mean.

**"And his weaning is in two years."** Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning the child is breastfed and weaned within two years after birth, and connects it with 2:233, "The mothers shall give suck to their children for two whole years, for those who desire to complete the term of suckling." On this basis Ibn ʿAbbas and other Imams understood that **the shortest possible period of pregnancy is six months**, since Allah says elsewhere "and the bearing of him, and the weaning of him is thirty months" (46:15). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful caveat: the two years mentioned here is in accordance with customary practice, and the ayah carries no ruling about any additional period of suckling; that discussion belongs to 46:15.

**"Give thanks to Me and to your parents. Unto Me is the final destination."** Ibn Kathir explains the closing clause as Allah's own guarantee: *I will reward you most generously for that.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the pairing directly: Allah has commanded us to be grateful to Him, and along with that, to be grateful and obedient to our parents.

## Ayah 15: the one place you do not obey them

"But if they strive with you to make you join in worship with Me others that of which you have no knowledge, then obey them not." Ibn Kathir: if they try hard to make you follow them in their religion, do not accept that from them — **but do not let that stop you from behaving with them in the world kindly**, that is, treating them with respect.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this Islam's peerless law of justice. When parents press a son or daughter towards shirk and kufr while Allah's command says otherwise, things become difficult, and one naturally fails to stay within limits; there was a real probability that in carrying out the divine injunction the child would use improper language or manners and so insult the parents. Islam is a just and equitable law, and here everything has a limit. So alongside the command not to obey them in matters of shirk comes *wa-ṣāḥibhumā fī'd-dunyā maʿrūfā* — "and be with them, in this world, with due fairness." Its explanation: in the matter of contravening your faith, do not obey them; but in worldly matters — serving them physically, financially, or in any other way needed — do not fall short. Deal with them according to recognised custom. Show them no disrespect. Do not respond to what they say in a manner that hurts them unnecessarily. **The pain you cause them by not accepting their insistence on shirk and kufr is something you will simply have to bear, since you have no choice there — but let that necessity stay within its functional limits, and keep abstaining from causing them pain in other matters.**

Then: "and follow the path of him who turns to Me in repentance and in obedience" — Ibn Kathir says this means **the believers**. If the parents' path is closed to you on this one point, you are not left without a path. And "then to Me will be your return, and I shall tell you what you used to do" — the final accounting is with Allah.

**Saʿd's story.** At-Tabarani recorded in *al-ʿIshrah* that Saʿd bin Malik said this ayah was revealed concerning him. He was a man who honoured his mother; when he became Muslim she said: O Saʿd, what is this new thing I see you doing? Leave this religion of yours, or I will not eat or drink until I die, and people will say shame on you for what you have done to me, and that you have killed your mother. He said: do not do that, O mother, for I will not give up this religion of mine for anything. She stayed a day and a night without eating and became exhausted; then another day and night, and she became utterly exhausted. When he saw that, he said: O my mother, by Allah, even if you had a hundred souls and they were to depart one by one, I would not give up this religion of mine for anything — so if you want to, eat, and if you want to, do not eat. So she ate.

Notice how he answers in that report: clearly and without wavering, yet still addressing her as his mother, without mockery and without abandoning her. That is ayah 15 lived out.

## Living it

- **Gratitude may be the wisdom itself.** On one of the two readings Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records for ayah 12, thankfulness *is* the ḥikmah Luqman was given, and gratitude is the greatest wisdom there is. Start there.
- **Give your children your best, not your leftovers.** Luqman gave the closest and most beloved of people to him the best of his knowledge — tawḥīd — first.
- **Guard the tongue.** By Luqman's own account, his standing came from always telling the truth and avoiding useless things.
- **Serve your mother concretely.** The ayah does not ask for sentiment; it recalls the months of carrying, weakness upon weakness, and the nights of feeding and staying awake.
- **Where a parent asks for disobedience to Allah, refuse the request without withdrawing the kindness.** Refusal is one thing; disrespect is another, and only the first is asked of you.

passages.title: Nothing escapes Allah: Luqman's charge to his son
passages.tafsir:
Luqman is still speaking to his son. These four ayat carry his advice from what a person must **believe**, to what he must **do**, to how he must **carry his own body** among other people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers them as Luqman's second through fifth bequests: belief in Allah's all-encompassing knowledge (ayah 16), the correction of one's own deeds and then of other people's (ayah 17), and finally social manners (ayat 18–19).

One thread ties them together. Because **nothing at all escapes Allah** — not a mustard seed's weight hidden in rock — **nothing at all is too small to matter**: not the tilt of your cheek when someone speaks to you, not the swagger in your step, not the volume of your voice. A father who has just taught his son that Allah brings forth what is hidden then tells him how to walk down a street. That is not a change of subject; it is the same lesson applied.

## Ayah 16 — "Even the weight of a mustard seed"

Luqman says that if a thing be *mithqāl ḥabbatin min khardal* — the **weight of a grain of mustard seed** — and it be in a rock, or in the heavens, or on the earth, Allah will bring it forth.

Ibn Kathir explains the unnamed "it" as **a wrong action or a sin** the size of a grain of mustard seed, and "Allah will bring it forth" as meaning He will bring it forth **on the Day of Resurrection**, when it is placed in the Scales of justice and everyone is rewarded or punished for his actions — if they are good he is rewarded, if bad he is punished. He connects this to two other ayat: *"And We shall set up Balances of justice on the Day of Resurrection, then none will be dealt with unjustly in anything"* (21:47), and *"So whosoever does good equal to the weight of a speck of dust shall see it. And whosoever does evil equal to the weight of a speck of dust shall see it"* (99:7–8).

Then Ibn Kathir's own comment on the hiding places the ayah names: even if this tiny thing were to be hidden inside a solid rock or anywhere in the heavens and the earth, Allah will bring it forth, "because nothing is hidden from Him, not even the weight of a speck of dust in the heavens or on the earth."

**"Verily, Allah is Laṭīf, Khabīr"** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as *Subtle, Well-Aware*. These are two of Allah's names, and Ibn Kathir keeps them precisely where the ayah puts them: in the domain of His knowledge. *Laṭīf*, he says, means His knowledge is **subtle**, for nothing is hidden from Him, no matter how small, subtle and minute. *Khabīr*, **Well-Aware**, he illustrates with an unforgettable image — Allah is aware "even of the footsteps of an ant in the darkest night."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens this into a point of creed. One must **irrevocably hold** the belief that Allah's knowledge surrounds every single particle of whatever there is in and around the expanses of the heavens and the earth, together with His most perfect power — nothing can hide from His knowledge and view: not the smallest of the small that is not commonly visible, nor the farthest of the far, nor what lies behind layers upon layers of darkness and curtains. And He can, when He wills, cause it to be present where He wills. This all-covering knowledge and power, Maʿārif adds, is in its own place **a basic belief of Islam — and certainly a great proof of Tawḥīd**, the belief in the Oneness of Allah.

Sit with what this does to a person's inner life. If nothing is hidden from Him, not even the weight of a speck of dust, then there is no such thing as a deed too small to be brought forth — in either direction. The tiny good you did where no one saw is on the record. So is the tiny wrong.

## Ayah 17 — the deed that anchors every deed, then the duty owed to others

**"O my dear son, establish the prayer."** Ibn Kathir glosses this as offering the prayer **properly, at the appointed times**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks why, out of all the obligatory deeds, only Salah is named here. Its answer: Salah is the greatest and most important of them, and not simply important in itself — it is the **master deed**, the one that becomes the catalyst changing other deeds towards the better, as the Qur'an says of it, *"Surely the prayer restrains from shamelessness and evil"* (29:45). So out of the obligatory good deeds, mentioning Salah was considered sufficient.

There is also a point in the verb. The Arabic is *aqim* — **"establish"** — not merely "making" or "saying" or "doing" it. Maʿārif notes that English has no exact equivalent; the term *iqāmah* includes **all the attending considerations**: performing the prayer with due respect to its essentials and manners, fully and faithfully; observing punctuality in its timings; and being consistent in fulfilling its requisites.

**"…and enjoin the good, and forbid the evil."** Ibn Kathir adds the crucial qualifier: **to the best of your ability and strength**. Maʿārif frames the logic: Islam is a collective religion, and the betterment of the community, along with the betterment of the individual, is an important part of its social system — so this duty was mentioned alongside a duty as weighty as the Salah. Two duties stand here: **make yourself better**, and **make others better**. Both, says Maʿārif, need a lot of restraint and hard work, and facing those difficulties and remaining firm is no easy task.

**"…and be patient over what befalls you."** The placement is deliberate. Ibn Kathir says Luqman knew that whoever enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil will **inevitably** encounter harm and annoyance from people, so he told his son to be patient. Maʿārif says the same: those who stand to serve people by telling them what is good for them receive nothing but opposition and hostility in return — and so, alongside the recommendation, patience was recommended too.

This is a father protecting his son from disillusionment. He does not promise that speaking up will be welcomed. He tells him the harm is coming, and hands him the tool for it in advance.

**"Verily, that is among the matters of firm resolve"** (*ʿazm al-umūr*). Ibn Kathir: being patient when people cause harm or annoyance is **one of the most important commandments**. Maʿārif renders the phrase as "among the matters of determination" — the things that take a settled, resolved will, not a passing mood.

## Ayat 18–19 — how a believer occupies a room

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts **four points of social manners** in these two ayat: (1) the prohibition of talking to and meeting with people with the face turned arrogantly; (2) the prohibition of walking haughtily on Allah's earth; (3) the instruction to be moderate in one's walking; and (4) the prohibition of talking very loudly. Together they describe how a believer holds himself in public.

### The turned cheek (ayah 18)

*Wa lā tuṣaʿʿir khaddaka li'n-nās* — "and do not turn your cheek away from people." Maʿārif opens the word for us. *Lā tuṣaʿʿir* is a derivation from **ṣaʿara**, which is **a disease among camels that causes a tilt in the neck** — similar, Maʿārif says, to the stroke among human beings that makes the face become crooked. From there it carries the sense of turning one's face away in disdain.

Feel what the vocabulary has done. The arrogant man's little sideways tilt of the face — the gesture of someone too important to look at you — is named with the word for **a sick animal's deformity**. Maʿārif's conclusion: do not turn your face away from people when you meet them and talk to them, for it is a sign of avoidance and arrogance and very much against the norms of gentle manners.

Ibn Kathir's gloss is the same, and adds the positive replacement: do not turn your face away from people when you speak to them or they speak to you, looking down on them in an arrogant fashion — rather **be gentle towards them and greet them with a cheerful face**. In support he quotes a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ; the source before me gives only a fragment of it and names no collection, so I quote it as it stands: *"…even if it is only by greeting your brother with a cheerful countenance. And beware of letting your lower garment trail below your ankles, for this is a kind of boasting, and Allah does not like boasting."*

### The swaggering walk (ayah 18)

*Wa lā tamshi fi'l-arḍi maraḥan.* Maʿārif defines *maraḥ* as **walking proudly, with assumed airs**. Its rebuke is beautifully argued: Allah has given this earth the lowest profile from among the entire range of elements He created — is it not that you were born from it, and on it you walk around? **Know your reality, and do not walk haughtily.** This, it says, is the way of the arrogant. Ibn Kathir puts it more bluntly still: do not be boastful, arrogant, proud and stubborn; do not do that, "for Allah will hate you." He brings the parallel from Sūrah al-Isrā': *"And walk not on the earth with conceit and arrogance. Verily, you can neither rend nor penetrate the earth nor can you attain a stature like the mountains in height"* (17:37).

The ayah closes: **"Verily, Allah likes not any arrogant boaster"** (*mukhtāl fakhūr*). Ibn Kathir explains this as the one who **shows off and admires himself, feeling that he is better than others**. Note that the ayah does not merely forbid the walk; it tells you how Allah regards the man who walks that way.

### The measured pace (ayah 19)

**"And be moderate in your walking."** Ibn Kathir: walk in a moderate manner, neither slow and lazy nor excessively fast, but somewhere in between these two extremes.

Maʿārif works out both edges. **Too fast**: walking in haste or helter-skelter goes against decorum and dignity — and it quotes a hadith, citing *al-Jāmiʿ aṣ-Ṣaghīr* from Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah ؓ, that making too much haste in walking ruins the radiance of the believer; besides, in such a manner of walking there remains the likelihood of hurting oneself or someone else. **Too slow**: an exaggeratedly slow gait is, Maʿārif says, the habit of the arrogant and the ostentatious who like to impress people with their distinct class — that mode it rules **ḥarām**; or it is the habit of women, who do not walk fast due to their natural modesty, which for a man is not permissible if the intention is to strike a semblance with them and, even without that intention, remains a defect in men; or it is the habit of the sick who walk so out of compulsion, and a healthy man who stoops to feign the looks of the sick is showing **ungratefulness to Allah**.

Two reports fill this out. Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd ؓ said that the noble Companions were **prohibited from walking hurriedly** (as if running) like the Jews and **from walking very slowly** (as if crawling) like the Christians, and were ordered to take a moderate gait in between the two.

And Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah ؓ, seeing a man walking very slowly as if he were going to fall dead, asked why he walked like that. She was told he was one of the *qurrā'* — the plural of *al-qāri'*, one trained to recite the Qur'an according to its phonetics; in those days, Maʿārif explains, the title also covered someone who combined mastery of authentic recitation and its etiquette with being a perfect scholar of the Qur'an. Her reply: **ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ؓ was a lot more of a "qāri'" than this man**, yet his habit was to **walk swiftly** when he walked — Maʿārif clarifies this means a functional swiftness, not the post-haste walking that is prohibited — and when he talked, he talked in a manner that people would hear him well. The man ʿĀ'ishah held up as by far the greater *qāri'* moved and spoke like someone with work to do.

### The lowered voice (ayah 19)

**"And lower your voice."** Ibn Kathir: do not exaggerate in your speaking and do not raise your voice unnecessarily. Maʿārif adds the other side, taking ʿUmar ؓ as the model again: "lowering" means not raising your voice **any more than necessary**, and not shouting — while ʿUmar's own way was to talk so that his audience could hear him without having to put any strain on their ears, not at a pitch so low that they would have to ask him to repeat himself.

Then the closing image: **"Verily, the ugliest of voices is the braying of the donkeys."** Mujahid and others said the most ugly of voices is the voice of the donkey — meaning that when a person raises his voice, the resulting noise is like the voice of a donkey in its loudness; and moreover, this is hateful to Allah.

Ibn Kathir draws a legal inference from the comparison. Likening a loud voice to that of a donkey implies that it is **forbidden and extremely blameworthy** — and his evidence is the Prophet's ﷺ own words: *"It is not befitting us to be an evil parable. The person who takes back his gift, he is like a dog that vomits and then goes back to his vomit."* If the Prophet ﷺ recoiled from believers being described by such a likeness, then having your voice named alongside a donkey's is no light rebuke.

## The Prophet ﷺ as the living form of this advice

Maʿārif notes that all of these virtues were already part of the habits and traits of the Prophet ﷺ, and cites the *Shamā'il* of Tirmidhī: Sayyidnā Ḥusayn ؓ said that he asked his father, Sayyidnā ʿAlī al-Murtaḍā ؓ, about the manner in which the Prophet ﷺ interacted with the people he sat with. He answered that he ﷺ was **always cheerful, naturally obliging, gentle** — neither impolite nor rude, **not clamorous** or immodest, no faultfinder and no miser; he would remain indifferent to what he did not like, yet would not make others become distracted from it if it was lawful and desirable for them to have, and would not say anything that would stop others from having what he did not want — instead he would observe silence. And three things he had left out for good: **disputation, arrogance, and indulgence with what was unnecessary and not worth doing**.

Lay that description over ayat 18–19 and the lines meet: the cheerful face against the turned cheek, the absence of clamour against the raised voice, arrogance abandoned against *maraḥ*.

## More of Luqman's wisdom

Ibn Kathir observes that this advice is told to us by Allah **so that people may follow it and take it as a good example**, and he adds some other proverbs and words of advice narrated from Luqman, as basic principles.

Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn ʿUmar said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Luqman the Wise used to say: when something is entrusted to the care of Allah, He protects it."*

It was narrated that As-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā said that Luqman told his son: **"Wisdom puts the poor in the company of kings."**

And it was narrated that ʿAwn ibn ʿAbdullāh said that Luqman told his son: "O my son! When you come to a gathering of people, greet them with *salām*, then **sit at the edge of the group**, and do not speak until you see that they have finished speaking. Then if they remember Allah, join them; but if they speak of anything else, then leave them and go to another group."

## Living it

- Stop treating small deeds as negligible. Ayah 16 says the mustard-seed weight is brought forth — nothing is hidden from Him, in either direction.
- Move your prayer from merely *done* to *established*: with its essentials and manners fully and faithfully, punctual in its timings, consistent in its requisites (Maʿārif on *iqāmah*).
- When you call others to good, budget for the friction. Ibn Kathir says the harm is inevitable; patience is issued with the command, not after it.
- Face people when they speak to you, and meet them with a cheerful face — Ibn Kathir makes that the direct replacement for the arrogant tilt.
- Walk moderately — neither slow and lazy nor excessively fast.
- Speak at the volume your listener actually needs: not more than necessary, and not so low that they must strain to hear you.

passages.title: Lavish favours met with blind imitation
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat set an enormous act of generosity beside an astonishingly small excuse. In ayah 20 Allah spreads out before mankind the whole furnished universe — everything in the heavens and everything on the earth put to work in their service — and blessings poured over them until nothing is lacking, outward and inward alike. Then, in the same breath, He notes that some people still argue about Him with nothing in their hands; and in ayah 21, when invited to follow what He has sent down, their entire answer is: *this is what we found our fathers doing.* The unity of the passage is that contrast: lavish, unearned favour on one side; on the other, a refusal to think, defended by nothing but habit.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out how deliberately these ayat are placed. The surah opened by rebuking the disbelievers and idolaters for clinging to their kufr and shirk even after they had seen the manifestations of Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and His most perfect power; against them, the obedient believers were praised and their good end described. The bequests of Luqmān (peace be upon him) that fill the middle of the surah were, as Maʿārif puts it, in a way a complement of that same subject. Now the text reverts to where it began — Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and power, His bounties and favours showered on His creation — and turns it all into a single exhortation: believe in the principle of His Oneness. So ayah 20 is not a change of topic after Luqmān's advice; it is the argument returning, enriched, to its main claim.

## "Subjected for you" — what *sakhkhara* actually means

The passage turns on the word **sakhkhara lakum** (سَخَّرَ لَكُم), "He subjected for you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word is well known and means to make something subservient to someone — and then raises the obvious objection honestly, because an ordinary reader feels it immediately: *not even everything on the earth is subservient to human will and command.* In fact, many things act counter to human choice. And as for the things of the heavens particularly, there is just about no probability of their being subservient to human beings at all. So in what sense are they "subjected"?

Maʿārif's answer opens the word up. Subjugation, in its real sense, is to force something into doing a particular job in a state of virtual compulsion. To say that the whole creation of the heavens and the earth has been subjugated for human beings means that this entire range of creation was **yoked into their service**, to bring all sorts of benefits to them. Out of these things, many were additionally put under human command, so that a person can use them as and when he wishes. But other things have been commissioned to serve us — which they do — without ever being made subject to human command: the heavenly creations, planets, stars, lightning, rains, and similar others.

And that, Maʿārif argues, is the dictate of Divine wisdom rather than a gap in the gift. Had those things been subjugated to follow human orders, they would have been affected by human temperaments, tastes and varying conditions. One person would have wanted the sun to rise early, while another's need would have it rise later. Someone would have asked for rain, while another, travelling through an open field, would have opted for no rain. Such divergent demands would have triggered operational malfunction in the workings of the universal heavenly system. Therefore Allah put all these things into the service of human beings but did not make them subject to their will and command — and this too, Maʿārif concludes, is in a way subjugation. *Allah knows best.*

This is worth sitting with. The favour in ayah 20 is not that the universe takes instructions from us; it is that it works for us reliably, without us, and often against our stated preferences at any given moment. The sun that will not rise when you ask it to is serving you better than a sun that would.

## What exactly has been put to work for you

Ibn Kathir fills in the inventory, and the sheer ordinariness of the list is the point. In the heavens, Allah has subjugated for them the stars, which give them light during the night and during the day; He has created the clouds, the rain, the snow and the hail; and He has made the heavens a canopy which covers and protects them. On the earth He has created for them stability, and rivers, trees, crops and fruits. Here, Ibn Kathir says, Allah reminds His creation of the blessings He bestows upon them in this world and the Hereafter.

Notice how the ayah addresses this: **"See you not…"** It does not begin a new lesson. It asks you to look again at what has been in front of your eyes your whole life. The evidence for Tawhid in this passage is not exotic; it is the sky over your head and the ground under your feet.

## *Asbagha* — poured out to the last fill

The second half of ayah 20 says Allah **asbagha** His blessings upon you, "outward and inward." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word **isbāgh** (اسباغ) as meaning to perfect, to make complete, to provide in great abundance to the last fill. It is not the language of a measured ration. It is the language of something poured until it overflows.

Then the ayah divides those blessings into two kinds, **ẓāhirah** (outward) and **bāṭinah** (inward), and Maʿārif fills out the two categories:

**Outward — what the senses register.** Maʿārif gives, as examples, the beauty of shape and the symmetry of the human limbs, made into such proportion as would allow maximum functional movement while causing no disfigurement of one's shape and looks. Then provisions, property, wealth, avenues of economic opportunity, health and well-being. And then — significantly — it places under this same heading things a modern reader might not have thought to count as "outward": that the religion of Islam has been made easy to follow, that a person is *enabled* to obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, the ascendancy of Islam over other faiths, and the support given to Muslims encountering enemies.

**Inward — what belongs to the heart.** Maʿārif lists īmān (faith), *maʿrifah* (knowing Allah), intellect, reason, good morals — and two that are easy to miss because they consist of something *not* happening to you: the good fortune of having one's sins left unexposed, and of one's crimes not being punished instantly. Every day that your worst moments stay hidden and your disobedience goes unpunished is itself a favour being poured out on you.

Ibn Kathir names what the completing and perfecting of the favour consisted of: Allah completed and perfected His graces upon them, apparent and hidden, **by sending Messengers, revealing Books, and removing doubts and excuses.** That is the hinge of the whole passage. Revelation is not presented as a demand made on top of the blessings; revelation is itself counted among the blessings — the one that closes off every excuse. Which is precisely why the answer given in ayah 21 is so damning.

Maʿārif closes its comment on this ayah by admitting defeat before the subject: the manifestations of Allah's knowledge, power and blessings are endless. They cannot be encompassed by anyone through speech, nor can any pen write them comprehensively.

## The three empty hands

"Yet of mankind is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or a Book giving light."

Ibn Kathir specifies what the dispute is *about*: those who dispute concerning Allah — that is, His **Tawhid** (His Oneness), and His sending the Messengers. And he specifies what the disputers have to stand on: their dispute is without knowledge, and they have no sound evidence or valid inherited Book. He brings the parallel wording of another ayah — "And among men is he who disputes about Allah, without knowledge or guidance, or a Book giving light (from Allah)" (22:8) — glossing "giving light" (*munīr*) as **clear and unambiguous.**

Read the three negations as three doors closed in sequence. *Knowledge* — something you worked out and verified for yourself. *Guidance* — something a true guide handed to you. *A luminous Book* — a revealed scripture, clear and unambiguous, standing behind your claim. A person arguing against Allah's Oneness has none of the three. And Ibn Kathir's phrase "valid inherited Book" is pointed: even the appeal to something received from earlier generations is ruled out here. Their hands are simply empty.

## "This is what we found our fathers doing"

Ayah 21 gives the disputers a fair invitation and records their reply. Ibn Kathir explains that "when it is said to them" means to *these* people, the ones who dispute about the Oneness of Allah; and that "follow that which Allah has sent down" means **the pure Divine Laws that He has sent down to His Messengers**. So the invitation is not to a tribe, a personality, or a new custom. It is to what came down from above.

Their answer: *"Nay, we shall follow that which we found our fathers (following)."* Ibn Kathir's comment cuts to the bone — **they have no other proof except the fact that they are following their forefathers.** That is the entire case. Not that the fathers were right; not that the fathers had evidence; only that the fathers were the fathers.

And Allah has already answered that argument elsewhere, as Ibn Kathir notes by citing the words: "Even though their fathers did not understand anything nor were they guided" (2:170). His paraphrase of the challenge is worth having as he frames it: what do you think, you who take the forefathers' deeds as proof — that they were misguided, and you are following in their footsteps? Inheritance transmits the practice; it does not transmit its truth. If the fathers had no understanding and no guidance, then to imitate them is not loyalty, it is repeating a mistake with more people involved.

## "Even if Shayṭān invites them to the torment of the Fire?"

The passage ends with a question rather than a verdict, and the question is devastating: would you still follow, even if Shayṭān were the one inviting them — and inviting them to the torment of the Fire?

This exposes what blind imitation really is. The imitator believes he is following his fathers. But the ayah asks him to look further up the chain: who put that practice into the fathers' hands in the first place? A path that no knowledge, no guidance, and no luminous Book supports did not appear from nowhere. And the invitation it carries — however warm and familial it feels in the moment — terminates at the Fire. The imitator never intended that destination. That is exactly why the Qur'an makes him look at it.

## Living it

**Look again at what you have stopped seeing.** The passage's own method is "see you not…" — pointing not to marvels far away but to the stars, the rain, the canopy of the sky, the rivers and crops and fruits, a body proportioned so that it moves fully without losing its form. Gratitude here begins as attention.

**Count the inward favours too.** Maʿārif's inward list — faith, knowing Allah, intellect, reason, good morals, sins left unexposed, crimes not punished instantly — will never appear in any tally you make of your own blessings unless you deliberately put them there. Some of the greatest favours in your life are things that quietly did not happen to you.

**Treat revelation as part of the gift.** Ibn Kathir's phrasing — that the graces were completed and perfected by sending Messengers, revealing Books, and removing doubts and excuses — reframes the command in ayah 21. "Follow what Allah has sent down" is not the bill arriving after the banquet; it is the last and best course of it.

**Audit your reasons.** The test in these ayat is not whether a practice is old or inherited, but whether, when asked *why*, you can point to knowledge, to guidance, or to what Allah sent down — and not merely to the fact that this is how it has always been done around you. Ayah 21 does not condemn them for honouring their fathers; it condemns them for having no other proof at all. Custom is a fine servant and a catastrophic proof.

passages.title: The firmest handhold, and a brief respite for deniers
passages.tafsir:
