These three ayat draw the line the sūrah has been moving toward: on one side, the person who hands himself over to Allah and does good, who is described as having grasped the most trustworthy handhold; on the other, the person who refuses — whose refusal the Prophet ﷺ is told not to grieve over, and whose enjoyment in this world is called *little* before a great torment. Ayah 22 gives the believer's grip, ayah 23 tells the Prophet ﷺ where the deniers' case is actually being settled, and ayah 24 says what happens at the end of the little while.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene briefly. The sūrah opened by admonishing the disbelievers and idolaters for still persisting in their disbelief and shirk **even though** they had seen the manifestations of Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and His most perfect power; in contrast, obedient believers were praised and their good end was mentioned. The bequests of Luqmān that fill the middle of the sūrah were, in a way, a complement of that same subject. Then, just before our passage, the text returns to Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and power, to His bounties and favours showered on His creation, and to the call to believe in His Oneness.

Ayat 22–24 are the human response to that reminder. Two people stand in the same world, under the same bounties; the ayat tell you what separates them and how each one ends.

## Ayah 22: submitting the face, and doing it beautifully

**"Whoever submits his face (himself) to Allah, while he is a *muḥsin*, has grasped the most trustworthy handhold."**

Two things are named, and the ayah holds them together.

**Submitting the face.** In Arabic, offering your *wajh* — your face — stands for offering the person, which is why the translation renders it "submits himself." Ibn Kathir unpacks it in three strokes: he **does deeds sincerely for Allah's sake**, he **submits to His commandments**, and he **follows His Law**. So the inward direction of the heart and the outward compliance of the limbs are both included, pointed at the same One.

**While he is a *muḥsin*.** *Iḥsān* is doing a thing well, beautifully, to a standard. Ibn Kathir defines the *muḥsin* here with plain edges: **doing what his Lord has commanded, and abstaining from what He has forbidden.** So this is not a vague warmth of feeling. It is a life shaped by a command and a prohibition — and, in the wording of the ayah, it is a state he is in ("while he is"), not an occasional act.

**The most trustworthy handhold.** The ayah's own picture is of a hand closing on something and holding it. And what does that grip actually secure? Ibn Kathir is remarkably direct: **he has received a firm promise from Allah that He will not punish him.** That is what makes the handhold trustworthy — not the strength of the hand, but the reliability of the One who gave the promise. A believer who feels his own grip trembling should notice that the ayah's security is anchored at the other end.

**"And to Allah return all matters for decision."** Ayah 22 closes by lifting the frame. Every affair — the believer's and the denier's, the ones that look settled and the ones that look lost — returns to Allah for its decision. That closing line is the hinge into ayah 23.

## Ayah 23: a word to the Prophet ﷺ about grief

**"And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you. To Us is their return, and We shall inform them what they have done."**

Ibn Kathir renders the sense as: *do not grieve over them, O Muhammad ﷺ, because they disbelieve in Allah and in the Message you have brought, for their return will be to Allah and He will tell them what they used to do* — which, Ibn Kathir adds, means **He will punish them for it.**

Notice the shape of the consolation. The sorrow being addressed is the grief of a man watching people refuse what he has brought them. Allah does not rebuke the feeling; He removes its cause by telling His Messenger ﷺ where the matter is actually being handled. Their return is to Allah, and the accounting is His to give, not the Prophet's ﷺ to force.

**"Verily, Allah is the All-Knower of what is in the breasts."** Ibn Kathir's comment is a single line: **and nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him.** The ayah does not say Allah knows what is *said* or what is *done*, but what is in the *breasts* — the interior of a person.

That lands here for a reason, standing between the two halves of the passage. For the denier, it means no concealment succeeds. For the *muḥsin* of ayah 22, it means the sincerity Ibn Kathir put first in his definition of submission is not a private effort going unseen — the One who holds the other end of the handhold is the One from whom nothing whatsoever is hidden.

## Ayah 24: a little while, then a great torment

**"We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment."**

Ibn Kathir moves word by word.

**"We let them enjoy for a little while"** — this is, he says, **in this world**. Everything the deniers have is inside that clause. It is called enjoyment, so the Qur'an is not pretending their comfort is unreal; and it is called *little*.

**"Then in the end We shall oblige them"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this as **"We shall cause them."** They are brought to it; the wording gives them no say. That is the reverse of their situation during the little while, when they choose freely and answer to no one.

**"To a great torment"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as **a torment that is terrifying and difficult to bear.**

Ibn Kathir then places a parallel ayah alongside it, from Sūrah Yūnus: *"Verily, those who invent a lie against Allah, will never be successful." Enjoyment in this world! and then unto Us will be their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment because they used to disbelieve* (10:69–70). The same three beats in the same order: a brief enjoyment, a return, a severe punishment.

It is worth holding ayah 24 beside what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān had just been describing — Allah's blessings perfected on people, outward and inward. The outward ones it names are the ones we register with our senses: the proportion and symmetry of the human frame, provision, property, wealth, avenues of earning, health and well-being. The inward ones belong to the heart: faith, *maʿrifah* (knowing Allah), intellect and reason, good morals, and the good fortune of having one's sins left unexposed and one's offences not punished on the spot. Ayah 24 says plainly that the deniers are enjoying too — and calls their portion *little*. Comfort, then, is not the measure. Ayah 22 already told us what the measure is.

## Living it

**Check both halves of what ayah 22 requires.** Ibn Kathir's two definitions are a usable audit: is this deed genuinely for Allah's sake, and is it inside what He commanded and clear of what He forbade?

**Let the promise carry your weight.** If the security of the handhold is, as Ibn Kathir says, a firm promise from Allah that He will not punish, then the answer to spiritual anxiety is to hold on more deliberately, not to doubt the hold.

**Learn what ayah 23 does with grief over other people's refusal.** The grief is real and the Prophet ﷺ felt it. But the ayah redirects it: their return is to Allah, He will inform them of what they did, and He knows what is in their breasts. Your work is the calling; the verdict is not filed with you. That frees a believer from both despair and self-appointed judgement.

**Read prosperity correctly.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's list shows how much of what we call blessing is outward and perceptible. Ayah 24 shows that outward comfort is exactly what the deniers are given for a little while. So a life can be full of the outward blessings and empty of the inward ones the commentary names — faith, knowing Allah, sound character.

**Keep the endings in view.** Ayah 22: to Allah return all matters for decision. Ayah 23: to Us is their return. Ayah 24: then a great torment. Three times in three ayat, the passage refuses to let us judge anything by its middle.

passages.title: They admit the Creator; His words never run out
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close an argument the surah has been building from its opening: the people who rejected the Prophet ﷺ already knew, and would admit under questioning, that Allah alone made the heavens and the earth — and yet they worshipped others alongside Him. Ayah 25 exposes that contradiction, ayah 26 states who the universe actually belongs to and what kind of Lord owns it, and ayah 27 lifts the eye from the created world to the Creator's own knowledge, which no amount of ink and no number of pens could ever write down. What holds the passage together is a single movement: from what they concede, to what that concession really implies, to how far beyond their grasp the One they conceded to actually is.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The surah opened by rebuking those who persisted in disbelief and in shirk — associating partners with Allah — even after seeing the manifestations of His all-encompassing knowledge and His most perfect power. Against them, the obedient believers were praised and their good end mentioned. The counsel of Luqman (peace be upon him) to his son sat in between as, in a way, a complement to the same subject. Now, in these ayat, the text returns to where it began: Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and power, His bounties and favours showered on His creation, and an exhortation to believe in His Oneness. So ayah 25 is not a new subject. It is the surah's opening charge brought back and closed.

## Ayah 25: the admission that convicts them

"And if you ask them: 'Who has created the heavens and the earth,' they will certainly say: 'Allah.'"

Ibn Kathir puts the point plainly: these idolaters, who associated others with Allah, admitted that Allah alone, with no partner or associate, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth — and then went on worshipping others besides Him, beings they themselves recognised were created by Him and subjugated to Him. That is the whole indictment in one sentence. Their shirk was never a rival theory of origins. It sat on top of a truth they already conceded.

And Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion: **by their admitting that, proof is established against them.** They are not condemned on evidence they never saw. They are condemned out of their own mouths.

**"Say: All the praises and thanks be to Allah."** The instruction to the Prophet ﷺ is striking. He is not told to argue further. He is told to praise. When the decisive point has been conceded, the reply is *al-ḥamdu lillāh* — praise belongs to Allah, that the truth has come out and the proof now stands. It is also a reminder of who deserves the gratitude they have been directing elsewhere.

**"But most of them know not."** They know the fact and miss its meaning. They can name the Creator and still not see that naming Him settles the question of who alone deserves worship. This is one of the quiet warnings of the passage: information about Allah is not the same as knowledge of Him. A person can hold a correct belief and draw no consequence from it at all.

## Ayah 26: whose world this is, and what kind of Owner He is

**"To Allah belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and covers everything: *He created it and has dominion over it.* Creation and ownership are not separate claims. The One who brought a thing into being owns it and disposes of it. Which means the objects of their worship were not merely made by Allah; they remain under His dominion. Nothing in the sky or on the earth stands outside that.

Then the two names that seal the ayah.

**Al-Ghanī** — the One free of all need. Ibn Kathir: *He has no need of anyone or anything besides Himself, and everything else is in need of Him.* The need runs in one direction only. When we turn to Him, we are the needy party, and He is not.

**Al-Ḥamīd** — the One worthy of all praise. Ibn Kathir explains: He is worthy of praise for all that He has created, so praise be to Him in the heavens and on earth for all that He has created and decreed, and He is worthy of praise **in all affairs**. That last phrase is worth sitting with. Not only in the affairs we find pleasant — in all of them. His decree is praiseworthy because of who decreed it, not only because of how it feels to us.

Put the two names together and the shape of the ayah becomes clear. He needs nothing from anyone, and He is worthy of praise for everything He has created and decreed. That is why *al-ḥamdu lillāh* in ayah 25 and *al-Ḥamīd* in ayah 26 echo one another: the praise commanded of the believer is simply the truth of who Allah already is.

## Ayah 27: the pens, the seas, and the Words that do not run out

### The occasion of revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir, reports that as it appears in some narratives, this ayah was revealed in response to a question posed by Jewish priests — and the background makes the ayah come alive.

Earlier revelation had said: *"and you are not given but a little from the knowledge"* (al-Isrāʼ 17:85). When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, some Jewish priests visited him and confronted him about that verse: "You say that you have been given a little from the knowledge. Is this what you are saying about your people, or have you included us too?"

The Prophet ﷺ answered, "I mean all" — his own people, and the Jews and Christians as well.

They pressed harder, and their objection was a serious one: Allah has given us the Torah, which stands out as *an explanation of everything*. How can that be "a little"?

His reply drew the line exactly where it belongs. That too, he said, is but a little compared with the knowledge of Allah. And beyond that — even the total knowledge contained in the Torah is not known to you; what you go by is no more than a certain measure of what you need. So compared with the knowledge of Allah, the collective knowledge of all the Scriptures and all the Prophets is also nothing but a little.

It was to support that statement, the report says, that this ayah was revealed: *"And if all the trees on the earth were pens..."* The ayah is therefore not an abstract flourish. It came in support of what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had just said in a live exchange — and it answers a very human temptation, the temptation to think that because we hold a revealed book, we have the matter of divine knowledge more or less covered.

### The image itself

"And if all the trees on the earth were pens and the sea, with seven seas behind it to add to it, yet the Words of Allah would not be exhausted."

Ibn Kathir unpacks the picture: even if all the trees on earth were made into pens, and the sea were made into ink, and topped up with seven more like it, and they were used to write the Words of Allah showing His might, His attributes and His majesty — the pens would break and the ink would run dry, even if more were brought.

Two details are easy to misread, and both commentaries head them off.

**"Seven" is not a count.** Ibn Kathir states that the number seven is used to indicate a large amount; it is not to be taken literally, nor to be understood as referring to the seven oceans of the world — as was suggested by those who took this idea from Israelite stories, "which we neither believe nor reject." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: the seven seas referred to here do not mean that there are seven seas present elsewhere; the sense is *suppose this ocean were replenished with seven more oceans*, and even the number seven appears as part of the example, with no restriction intended.

**And the point survives any number you like.** Both commentaries cite the parallel ayah: *"Say: If the sea were ink for the Words of my Lord, surely the sea would be exhausted before the Words of my Lord would be finished, even if We brought like it for its aid"* (al-Kahf 18:109). Ibn Kathir says the words **bi-mithlihi** — "like it" — do not mean merely another one, but another like it and another and another, because there is no limit to the signs and Words of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the reasoning underneath, and it is clean: the oceans may be added one after the other, and be they seven or seven thousand, they shall still remain limited, while the Words of Allah are unlimited. How, then, can something limited make an all-encompassing coverage of what is unlimited? The similitude is not exaggeration. It is a demonstration that no quantity of a finite thing will ever close the gap.

### What "the Words of Allah" means here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that *kalimāt Allāh* — the Words of Allah — here means His knowledge and His wisdom, citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and Maẓharī, and that this includes the manifestations of Divine power and Divine blessings. Ibn Kathir approaches it from the same side: the ayah tells us of Allah's might, pride, majesty, His beautiful Names and sublime attributes, and His perfect Words which no one can encompass — no human being knows their essence or nature, or how many they are.

Read that carefully, because it fixes the passage's real subject. What overflows the ink is not a long list of sentences. It is Allah Himself as He has made Himself known — His knowledge, His wisdom, His power, His Names and attributes. And this ayah tells us plainly that what we affirm of Him, we do not encompass. Not knowing the essence, the nature, or the number of His Words is not a gap in our faith. It is the honest position of a finite creature before an infinite Lord.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān had already put the same conclusion in a single sentence, and it is the bridge into this ayah: **the manifestations of Allah's knowledge, power and blessings are endless — these cannot be encompassed by anyone through speech, nor can any pen write them comprehensively.** Ayah 27 is that sentence turned into an image you cannot forget.

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir quotes the Leader of Mankind and Seal of the Messengers ﷺ as saying:

> **"I cannot praise You enough; You are as You have praised Yourself."**

This is the perfect human response to ayah 27. The one who knew Allah best is the one who declares that his praise falls short. Only Allah's own words about Himself do Him justice. So when we praise Him, we lean on His self-description rather than on our own invention — and we do not imagine that our best words have reached Him as He deserves.

### Al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm

The ayah closes: **"Verily, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Wise."** Ibn Kathir explains that He is All-Mighty and has subjugated all things to His will, so nothing can prevent what He wills, and none can oppose or put back His decision; and that He is All-Wise in His creation, His commands, His Words, His actions, His laws and all His affairs.

That pairing matters at the end of an ayah about limitless knowledge. Might without wisdom would be frightening; wisdom without might would be helpless. The One whose knowledge exceeds every ocean of ink also has the power to enact it and the wisdom to enact it rightly.

## Living it

**Do not confuse admitting a truth with living by it.** Ayah 25 shows people giving the correct answer about the Creator and getting no benefit from it. The question for us is not whether we would say "Allah" if asked who made the heavens — of course we would — but whether our hopes, fears and requests actually go to Him alone, or get quietly distributed among created things that are, as Ibn Kathir says, themselves created by Him and subjugated to Him.

**Let the reflex be praise.** When Allah's truth becomes clear, ayah 25 teaches the response: *al-ḥamdu lillāh*. And because He is *al-Ḥamīd*, worthy of praise in all affairs, that reflex is not reserved for the outcomes we wanted.

**Hold your knowledge humbly.** The occasion of ayah 27 is a group of learned men who assumed their scripture gave them the whole picture. Whatever we have learned is a cup dipped from an ocean that no ocean of ink could describe. That should keep a student of knowledge both hungry and humble.

**Take courage from the same fact.** A Lord whose wisdom cannot be exhausted by the writing of every pen on earth is not short of ways out of your situation. *Al-ʿAzīz*: nothing can prevent what He wills, and none can oppose or put back His decision. *Al-Ḥakīm*: He is All-Wise in His creation, His commands and all His affairs. And *al-Ghanī*: He has no need of you or of anything you could give Him — you are the one in need of Him.

passages.title: Effortless resurrection proves He alone is the Truth
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat make a single argument. Ayah 28 states the claim — raising the whole of mankind costs Allah no more than creating one soul; ayat 29 and 30 then supply the proof and the conclusion: look at the night sliding into the day and the sun and moon running on their fixed course, and you will know that Allah alone is the Truth and everything called upon beside Him is falsehood. Power, knowledge and sole divinity are woven into one chain: **He can do it — He hears and sees and knows everything you do — therefore He, and no other, is real.**

## Where the passage begins

Ayah 28 lands immediately after the great similitude of ayah 27: if every tree on earth were a pen and the ocean were ink, replenished by seven more oceans, the Words of Allah would still not run out. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *kalimāt Allāh*, "the Words of Allah", here means His knowledge and wisdom — including the manifestations of His power and His blessings — citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and Mazharī. Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stress that "seven seas" is not a claim that seven such oceans exist somewhere; the number is part of the picture, not a limit. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the logic: oceans, whether seven or seven thousand, remain limited, and the limited can never encompass the unlimited. Ibn Kathir adds that the closing names of that ayah, All-Mighty and All-Wise, mean that Allah "has subjugated all things to His will, so nothing can prevent what He wills."

Hold that in mind, because ayah 28 turns the same infinity in the other direction. His knowledge is beyond exhausting — and His power is beyond straining.

## Ayah 28: "only as a single person"

*Mā khalqukum wa-lā baʿthukum illā ka-nafsin wāḥidah* — "The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as a single person."

Ibn Kathir's explanation is exact and worth reading slowly: **His creation and resurrection of all of mankind on the Day of Resurrection is, in relation to His power, like the creation and resurrection of a single soul; all of this is easy for Him.**

Notice the qualifier "in relation to His power". The ayah is not saying that a billion people are somehow one person. It is correcting the instinct we cannot help bringing from our own experience — that a bigger job takes more effort, more time, more material. That instinct is true of creatures, whose strength is finite and is spent as it is used. It is simply irrelevant to Allah. For One whose power is not a quantity that can be divided or drained, "all of you" and "one of you" come to the same thing.

Ibn Kathir supports the point from the Qur'an itself with three ayat, each showing that Allah's act needs no repetition, no build-up, no second attempt:

- **36:82** — "Verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is."
- **54:50** — "And Our commandment is but one, as the twinkling of an eye." Ibn Kathir comments: He only has to command a thing once and it happens; there is no need for Him to repeat it or confirm it.
- **79:13–14** — "But it will be only a single *Zajrah*. When behold, they find themselves on the surface of the earth, alive after their death."

That last one is the resurrection itself, described as a single event with no process: one *Zajrah*, and the whole of humanity is standing on the earth's surface. The command is one; the outcome is universal.

## Why the ayah ends with "All-Hearer, All-Seer"

Ayah 28 closes with *inna Allāha samīʿun baṣīr* — "Verily, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Seer." At first this can feel like a change of subject. Ibn Kathir shows that it is the same point carried from power into knowledge:

> "…just as He hears all that they say, so He also sees all that they do, as if He is hearing and seeing a single soul. His power over all of them is like His power over a single soul."

So the closing names repeat the argument in another key. Just as raising billions is not "harder" for Him than raising one, hearing billions of voices at once is not more crowded for Him than hearing one voice. Our own hearing and sight are the very picture of a finite capacity — one conversation at a time, one direction at a time. That is exactly why Ibn Kathir extends the same "single soul" comparison to His hearing and seeing: what is scarce in us is not scarce in Him.

There is a quiet warning in it too. If He hears and sees each of us as though each were the only one, then no deed is lost in the crowd on the Day everyone is raised together.

## Ayah 29: the proof you can watch happening

Having stated the claim, the passage turns to evidence — and it does not reach for anything exotic. *A-lam tara* — "Do you not see…?" The proof is overhead, every day of your life.

**"He merges the night into the day, and merges the day into the night."** Ibn Kathir explains the merging like this: **He takes from the night and adds to the day, so that the day becomes longer and the night shorter, which is what happens in summer when the days are longest; then the day starts to become shorter and the night longer, which is what happens in winter.**

This is a beautifully chosen sign. Nobody sees it happen. There is no moment when the day visibly seizes a portion of the night. Minute by minute, month by month, the borrowing is so gradual and so exact that it registers only as a season. It is total control exercised so smoothly that it looks like nothing at all — which sits perfectly beside what ayah 28 has just said about resurrection: effortlessness is not evidence of small power.

**"And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running its course for a term appointed."** On the phrase *ilā ajalin musammā*, Ibn Kathir reports two interpretations and, notably, accepts both:

1. Each runs **within its set limits** — a course it does not overstep.
2. Each runs **until the Day of Resurrection** — the term at which this whole order ends.

"Both meanings are correct," he says. And the first view, he notes, is supported by the hadith of Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) **in the Two Sahihs**, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Abū Dharr! Do you know where this sun goes?" Abū Dharr said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He ﷺ said: "It goes and prostrates beneath the Throne, then it seeks permission from its Lord, and soon it will be said: 'Go back from whence you came.'"

Take in what that hadith does to the picture. The sun is a servant that prostrates and asks permission. The ayah has already said as much with the word translated "subjected" (*sakhkhara*): the sun and moon are not powers, they are put to service. This is why the two readings sit together so comfortably. A thing that must seek permission to return clearly runs "within set limits", and a thing running on permission clearly runs only until permission is withdrawn.

Ibn Kathir then records, through **Ibn Abi Hatim**, a statement of **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "The sun is like flowing water, running in its course in the sky during the day. When it sets, it travels in its course beneath the earth until it rises in the east" — and he said the same is true of the moon. Ibn Kathir notes that its chain of narration is *ṣaḥīḥ*. It is a Companion describing the sun's course as continuous, ceaseless motion under a command it never breaks.

**"And that Allah is All-Aware of what you do."** Ibn Kathir links this to 22:70, "Know you not that Allah knows all that is in the heaven and the earth?", and draws out the logic: **Allah is the Creator who knows all things** — citing 65:12, "It is Allah Who has created seven heavens, and of the earth the like thereof."

That is the join between the astronomy and you. The One who runs the seasons and the orbits is not a distant mechanism; the same knowledge that governs the sun's course takes in what you did today. The passage travels from the sky to your deeds in half a line.

## Ayah 30: the verdict — the Truth and the falsehood

*Dhālika bi-anna Allāha huwa al-Ḥaqq* — "That is because Allah, He is the Truth, and that which they invoke besides Him is falsehood."

"That is because" ties this ayah back to everything just shown. Ibn Kathir: **He shows you His Signs so that you may know from them that He is the Truth — meaning He truly exists and is truly divine — and that all else besides Him is falsehood.**

Notice the two halves of *al-Ḥaqq* in that explanation. It is not only that Allah is real as opposed to imaginary; it is that His divinity is real. Falsehood, its opposite, is not merely a wrong choice of deity: what is called upon has no divinity in it at all. That is the tragedy named in the words *mā yadʿūna min dūnihi*, "what they call upon besides Him" — a call going out to something that cannot receive it.

Ibn Kathir then presses the point with the sharpest lines in the passage:

> "He has no need of anything else, but everything else is dependent on Him, because everything in heaven and on earth is created by Him and is enslaved by Him; none of them could move even an atom's weight except with His permission. If all the people of heaven and earth were to come together to create a fly, they would not be able to do so."

Set that beside ayah 28 and the architecture of the passage becomes visible. Allah raises the whole of creation as easily as one soul; the whole of creation, pooling every power it has, cannot produce a single fly. That is the distance between the Truth and the falsehood. And "none of them could move even an atom's weight except with His permission" answers the fear that sits underneath calling on others besides Him — the sense that these other things have leverage over your life, so they had better be kept happy. They have no leverage. They cannot stir without His permission.

**"And that Allah, He is the Most High, the Most Great."** On *al-ʿAliyy al-Kabīr*, Ibn Kathir says: **He is the Most High and there is none higher than Him, and He is the Most Great who is greater than everything; everything is subjugated and insignificant in comparison to Him.** That last clause answers ayah 29: the sun and moon were subjected — and, in Ibn Kathir's reading, so is everything else. Nothing that people call upon stands outside that service.

## Living it

**Stop measuring Allah's power by the size of the request.** Ayah 28 dismantles the assumption that a bigger job needs a bigger effort. If raising all of mankind is, in relation to His power, like raising one soul, then nothing you could ask for is "a lot to ask". Big and small are our categories, not His.

**Let the ordinary sky do its work.** Ayah 29 chose the lengthening of days and the running of the sun — signs so reliable that we stop noticing them. Their reliability is the argument, not an anaesthetic. Watch the light change with the season and read it as Ibn Kathir read it: something is taking from the night and adding to the day, precisely, continuously, unseen.

**Live as one who is heard and seen.** The names closing ayah 28 and ayah 29 are not decoration. His attention to you is not diluted by the number of others: it is as though He hears and sees a single soul, and He is All-Aware of what you do.

**Audit what you actually lean on.** Ayah 30 draws a hard line: on one side the Truth, needing nothing and holding everything; on the other whatever is called upon besides Him — which cannot make a fly or move an atom's weight without His permission. Whatever you quietly trust to secure your provision, your safety or your standing belongs on one of those two sides. The passage asks you to put it on the right one.

passages.title: Ships at sea and sincerity that fades ashore
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat hold up a single scene — a ship crossing open water — and ask us to watch it twice: once as evidence of Allah's power, and once as a mirror of the human heart. Ayah 31 shows the sea as a creation under command and names the two qualities that let a person read that sign. Ayah 32 puts a storm on that same sea, shows the passengers calling on Allah alone, and then follows them onto dry land to see what survives of it. The unit is held together by the sea: the sea that carries, the sea that terrifies, and the shore where the sincerity of the storm quietly fades.

## Ayah 31: water that was given the strength to carry

"See you not that the ships sail through the sea by Allah's grace that He may show you of His signs?"

Ibn Kathir puts the emphasis exactly where the ayah puts it. Allah, he says, is the One who has subjugated the sea so that ships may sail on it **by His command — that is, by His power**. And then he adds the sentence that turns a familiar sight into a wonder: *"For if He did not give the water the strength to carry the ships, they would not sail."*

That is worth sitting with. We are used to thinking of the sea as an obstacle that human ingenuity overcame — timber, sails, engines, navigation. Ibn Kathir reverses the account. The buoyancy is not something the water arranged for itself; it is a strength *given* to it. Water is soft and formless, and yet it holds up something heavy enough to carry people and cargo across open ocean. Every voyage that ends safely is a creation doing what it was commanded to do.

**"That He may show you of His signs."** Ibn Kathir glosses this in three words: *meaning, by His power*. Notice the purpose clause. The sailing of ships is not merely permitted by Allah; it is arranged so that you would *look*. The opening words — "See you not…" — are not asking whether you have ever visited a harbour. They are asking whether the sight ever landed.

## Who can actually read the sign

"Verily, in this are signs for every patient, grateful person" — *ṣabbār shakūr*.

The ayah does not say the signs are there for the clever, or the well-travelled, or the scientifically trained. It names two qualities, and Ibn Kathir defines them as a matched pair: *"every person who bears difficulty with patience and who gives thanks at times of ease."*

Two conditions of life, two responses. Hardship is met with *ṣabr* — patient endurance. Ease is met with *shukr* — thanks. Ibn Kathir's gloss covers both halves of an ordinary life, the hard stretch and the easy one, so that a person who has both is a person whose whole life is a response to Allah.

And this is why the placement matters. Look at what comes next: the storm arrives, which is the difficulty that calls for patience, and then the safe landing, which is the ease that calls for thanks. Ayah 31 names the two virtues; ayah 32 sets down the two situations that test them.

## Ayah 32: waves like mountains

"And when waves cover them like shades…"

Ibn Kathir explains the image plainly: **"meaning, like mountains or clouds."** Both pictures say the same thing. The wave is no longer beside the ship; it is above it, high and overhanging. The sea that had been given strength to carry them now towers over them — and the same power stands behind both.

At that moment something happens that the Qur'an returns to again and again: **"they invoke Allah, making their invocations for Him only."** Not a trace of partnership survives a wave like that.

Ibn Kathir connects this to two other passages that press the point further:

- **"And when harm touches you upon the sea, those that you call upon vanish from you except Him"** (17:67). The other objects of hope do not argue their case; they simply are not there.
- **"And when they embark on a ship…"** (29:65) — the same scene, which continues, as Ibn Kathir quotes below, into what happens on land.

There is a quiet teaching in this. In the storm, human beings do not *arrive at* worshipping Allah alone for the first time; it is what is left when everything else has fallen away. The crisis does not create it. It uncovers it.

## The shore: where sincerity quietly dies

"But when He brings them safe to land, there are among them those that stop in between."

Rescued, they neither carry the sincerity of the storm forward nor, at first, openly renounce it. Ibn Kathir's rendering is exact: *those that stop in between*. The vow is not repudiated; it is left unpaid.

**Mujahid** said this "refers to the disbelievers," and Ibn Kathir explains that Mujahid was in effect reading *muqtaṣid* — "those that stop in between" — to mean *denier*, on the strength of the parallel verse: **"But when He brings them safely to land, behold, they give a share of their worship to others"** (29:65). Put the two verses side by side and the middle position is unmasked: the half-hearted return to Allah after rescue is where the return to partners begins. In the wave they had no partners at all. On the beach the partners come back.

That is the moral geometry of the passage. Sincerity produced by fear is not yet, by itself, a settled faith. It is real while the wave hangs overhead — but the test the ayah stages is not the prayer in the storm. It is the walk up the beach.

## *Khattār, Kafūr* — the two words for what went wrong

"And Our Ayat are not denied except by every *Khattār Kafūr*."

**Khattār.** Ibn Kathir: *"Khattar means one who betrays or stabs in the back."* He names the authorities for this reading — **Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Malik narrating from Zayd bin Aslam** — and then defines it further: *"This word describes a person who, whenever he makes a promise, breaks his promise, and it refers to the worst form of treachery."*

Consider how carefully chosen that is. The ayah could have called this person merely a disbeliever, or a forgetful one. It calls him a betrayer — and Ibn Kathir's definition turns specifically on promise-breaking. And notice where the word falls: immediately after a scene of people calling on Allah with nothing held back, and then stopping in between once they were safe. Betrayal is not the breaking of an obligation that was never taken on; it is the breaking of one that was.

**Kafūr.** Ibn Kathir: *"one who denies blessings and does not give thanks for them, rather he forgets them and does not remember them."* Note that the definition ends in forgetting. This is not only the loud denier who argues against Allah. It is also the man who simply stops recalling that he was saved. The blessing of the safe landing gets absorbed into ordinary life, and before long it carries no more weight in his heart than the weather.

And now the pairing at the start of ayah 31 comes into focus. The one who reads the signs is *ṣabbār shakūr* — patient in hardship, grateful in ease. The one who denies them is *khattār kafūr* — a betrayer of promises, a denier of blessings. The same storm and the same shore test both. The difference between them is not what they did in the wave. It is what they did afterwards.

## A note on the sea earlier in this surah

It is worth noticing in passing that this surah has already used the ocean as an image. In ayah 27, if all the trees on earth were pens and the ocean, backed by seven more, were ink, the words of Allah would still not come to an end. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "the words of Allah" there means His knowledge and wisdom, which "includes the manifestations of Divine power and Divine blessings," and that "seven" is not a literal count but a way of saying *however many you add*. Read alongside our two ayat, the images rhyme: there the ocean is too small to write down what Allah knows; here the ocean carries ships only because He gave the water the strength to do so. The largest thing a person can look at is used, both times, to point at something immeasurably larger.

## Living it

**Test your worship against the shoreline, not the storm.** Anyone can be sincere under a wave the size of a mountain. Take the moment you were most frightened and most honest with Allah — the illness, the accident, the news that came at night — and ask what remains of it now that it is over. The passage is not condemning the prayer of fear; it is asking what happened to it.

**Refuse the middle position.** The one who "stops in between" is not a rebel. He is someone who slowed down and halted. That is what makes ayah 32 so uncomfortable: the failure it describes is not dramatic, it is a fading.

**Repay the rescue with remembrance.** Ibn Kathir defines *kafūr* as one who forgets a blessing and does not remember it. The opposite of that is not a grand act; it is deliberate recall. Name the deliverances you have been given and speak them back to Allah, so that they do not silently expire.

**Aim to be one who sees.** The signs, ayah 31 says, are for the *ṣabbār shakūr*. If the world looks flat and unremarkable, the deficiency this ayah points to is not in the world but in that pair of qualities. Patience in the hard stretch and gratitude in the easy one are not merely good behaviour — they are, on the wording of this ayah, the eyesight with which Allah's signs are seen.

passages.title: The Day no parent avails, and the keys of the unseen
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah Luqmān closes with two warnings that belong together: on the Day of Resurrection no parent and no child will be able to stand in for the other (ayah 33), and the future — including the timing of that Day — is locked away with Allah alone (ayah 34). All that is left is to prepare now. With ayah 34, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the sūrah ends.

## "O humanity" — and why "your Lord"

Ayah 33 addresses all people, believing and disbelieving alike — served notice, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that they will face Allah and be accountable before Him for their deeds on the Day of Judgment, and that they should be prepared for it.

The command is not "fear Allah" but **ittaqū rabbakum — be mindful of your *Lord*** — *Rabb*: the master who nourishes, sustains and cherishes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why. The fear asked for is not the fear you feel toward a beast or an enemy — why would you expect that kind of danger from the compassionate master who feeds and raises you? It is the fear that arises from the sublimity and awe of one's elders: the way a son "fears" his father, or a student his teacher. Neither is an enemy; neither means him harm. But their affectionate sublimity and awe reside in the heart, and it is from there that they make one obey. That, says the commentary, is what is wanted here — that the sublimity and awe of Allah should reign supreme over your heart so that you can obey Him, perfectly and easily.

## The Day no ransom is accepted

**"…and fear a Day when no father will suffice his son, nor will a son be sufficing his father in the least."**

Ibn Kathīr explains: even if a father *wanted* to offer himself as a sacrifice for his son, it would not be accepted from him — and the same applies if a son wished to sacrifice himself for his father. The bond is not denied; its *usefulness* that Day is. This is the deepest natural loyalty we know: if that bond cannot carry you, nothing will.

Ibn Kathīr records, from Wahb bin Munabbih, that ʿUzayr (peace be upon him) said: seeing the misfortune of his people, he grew so sad that he could not sleep, so he prayed to his Lord and fasted and called upon Him weeping. An angel came to him, and he asked whether the souls of the righteous would intercede for the wrongdoers, or fathers for their sons. The angel answered that on the Day of Resurrection all matters will be settled, Allah's dominion will be made manifest, and no exceptions will be made; no one will speak that Day except with the permission of the Most Merciful. No father will answer for his son, no son for his father, no man for his brother, no servant for his master. No one will care about anybody except himself, weeping for himself and carrying his own burden, and no one will carry the burden of another. This was recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim.

## An important qualification: which father, which son?

Read on its own, this could seem to contradict other verses. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī, addresses it directly. Elsewhere the Qurʼān teaches that families are joined together in the Hereafter: *"And those who believed and their children followed them in belief — We will join their children with them"* (52:21) — even though the children's deeds may not match the ranking of their parents' deeds, such is the barakah (blessing) of righteous parents that the children too are made to reach where their parents are; but this is on condition that the children are believers, even if their deeds suffered from some shortcomings. Likewise: *"the eternal gardens they enter, and the righteous of their fathers, spouses, and progeny as well"* (13:23), where "the righteous" refers to their being believers.

Both verses prove that where parents and children — and likewise husband and wife — share the common denominator of being believers, they *will* receive benefit from each other on the Day of Judgment; and there are several narrations of ḥadīth which report children interceding on behalf of their parents. Therefore, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, the rule in ayah 33 becomes operative where one of the two is a believer and the other a disbeliever: a believing father can neither remit nor reduce his disbelieving son's punishment nor bring him any benefit, and a believing son is of no avail to his disbelieving father. What carries across the gulf between two people that Day is faith, not blood.

## The grammar of a father's love

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān flags a fine point here.

The father's side — *lā yajzī wālidun ʿan waladih*, "no father will suffice his son" — is a **verbal sentence**. The child's side — *wa lā mawlūdun huwa jāzin ʿan wālidih* — is a **nominal sentence**, which in Arabic is more emphatic. Why the extra weight on the child's side? Because a father's love for his children is more intense; the love of children does not reach that level of intensity even in this mortal world. Both directions are negated, but the child's lack of ability to bring benefit is stated with added emphasis.

Second, the child is called **mawlūd**, "the born one," rather than the more usual **walad**. *Walad* is general and includes the children of one's children as well; *mawlūd* denotes one's own son specifically. The effect, says the commentary: when even the son from the very loins of the father would be of no avail to him, any expectations pinned on a grandson or great-grandson are futile.

## Two deceptions to watch for

The ayah closes: **"Verily, the promise of Allah is true — so let not this present life deceive you, nor let the chief deceiver deceive you about Allah."**

The first trap is the world itself — as Ibn Kathīr glosses it, do not let your feelings of contentment with this life make you forget about the Hereafter. Nothing has to lie to you for this to happen; contentment alone will do it.

The second is a person. **Al-gharūr**, "the chief deceiver," refers to Shayṭān — the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah. Ibn Kathīr explains his method: he makes promises and arouses false desires, but there is no substance to them, as Allah says, *"He makes promises to them and arouses in them false desires; and Shayṭān's promises are nothing but deceptions"* (4:120). Note where the deception is aimed — he deceives you *about Allah*.

## Ayah 34: the five keys of the unseen

**"Indeed, Allah — with Him is the knowledge of the Hour. He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware."**

Ibn Kathīr calls these **the keys of the Unseen**, whose knowledge Allah has kept for Himself, and no one else knows them unless Allah tells him about them. When the Hour will occur is not known to any prophet who was sent or any angel who is close to Allah — *"None can reveal its time but He"* (7:187). Similarly, no one but Allah knows when rain will fall; but when He issues the command, the angels entrusted with bringing rain know about it, as do those among His creation whom He wills should know. So too with the wombs: no one but He knows what is in them, but when He decrees whether it is to be male or female, blessed or doomed, the angels entrusted with that know about it, as do those He wills. No one knows what he will earn tomorrow with regard to this world or the Hereafter; and no one knows in what land he will die.

That last phrase, Ibn Kathīr adds, means no person knows where his resting place will be: on the land or in the sea, on a plain or in the mountains. In *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr*, al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū al-Qāsim aṭ-Ṭabarānī recorded that Usāmah bin Zayd said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Allah does not will that a person should die in a certain land but He gives him a reason to go there."*

Ibn Kathīr also relays Qatādah: there are things Allah has kept to Himself, not known to any angel close to Him or any prophet sent by Him — no one among mankind knows when the Hour will come, in which year or month, or whether by night or during the day; nor when rain will come; nor what is in the wombs, male or female; nor whether tomorrow's earning will be good or bad. *You do not know, O son of Ādam, when you will die; you might die tomorrow, you might be stricken by calamity tomorrow.*

## From the Sunnah

**Imām Aḥmad** recorded that Buraydah said he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: *"There are five things which no one knows except Allah,"* and then recite this ayah. Ibn Kathīr notes the chain of narrators for this ḥadīth is *ṣaḥīḥ*.

**Imām Aḥmad** also recorded that Ibn ʿUmar said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The Keys of the Unseen are five, which no one knows except Allah,"* followed by the ayah. Ibn Kathīr says this was recorded only by **al-Bukhārī**, who narrated it in the Book of the Rain Prayer in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, and again in his *Tafsīr* with a different chain from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmar.

**Al-Bukhārī**, in his *Tafsīr* of this ayah, narrated from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was standing before the people one day when a man came and asked him about *īmān* — *"to believe in Allah, His Angels, His Books, His Messengers and in the meeting with Him, and to believe in the Resurrection in the Hereafter"*; about *islām* — *"to worship Allah alone and not associate anything in worship with Him, to establish regular prayer, to pay the obligatory Zakāh, and to fast in Ramaḍān"*; and about *iḥsān* — *"to worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you."* Then he asked when the Hour would come. He ﷺ replied, *"The one who is asked about it does not know more than the one who is asking,"* mentioned some of its signs — when the servant woman gives birth to her mistress, and when the barefoot and naked become leaders of the people — and said that the timing of the Hour is one of the five things which no one knows except Allah, reciting this ayah. Then the man went away, and the Prophet ﷺ said, *"Bring him back to me"*; they went to bring him back but could not find him, and he ﷺ said: *"That was Jibrīl, who came to teach the people their religion."* Ibn Kathīr adds that al-Bukhārī also recorded it in the Book of Faith, and Muslim with several chains of narration.

## What "knowledge of the unseen" actually means

**The word.** These five are called *mafātiḥ al-ghayb* in Sūrah al-Anʿām — *"And with Him are the keys of the Unseen; no one knows them but He"* (6:59) — and *mafātīḥ al-ghayb* in ḥadīth. Both are plurals of *miftāḥ*, a key that opens locks: they signify the sources of the Unseen that unravel its information.

**Are these the only five?** No. That knowledge of the unseen is particular to Allah in the absolute sense is explicitly stated in this verse, and this has been the belief of the entire Muslim community from the earliest to the succeeding generations. Naming five is not meant as a restriction — otherwise it would pose a contradiction with *"Say: no one in the heavens and the earth has the knowledge of the Unseen except Allah"* (27:65). They are mentioned to highlight their special significance, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason, citing *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: things of the unseen that people are generally keen to find out are just these five, and these are exactly the ones astrologers and their kind pick up in order to display their supposed access. Some narrations report that someone asked the Prophet ﷺ about these five things, whereupon this verse was revealed.

**The key distinction.** A statement of the Prophet ﷺ is reported on the authority of Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with them): *"I have been given the keys to everything except the five"* — reported by Imām Aḥmad, as Ibn Kathīr notes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the words *"I have been given"* make the matter clear. Whatever the Prophet ﷺ knew of the unseen came *to* him, in the form of revelation from Allah. It is therefore not included under the definition of *ʿilm ul-ghayb*; it is *anbāʼ ul-ghayb* — **news** of the unseen, as the Qurʼān itself calls it: *"These are some reports from the Unseen which We reveal to you"* (11:49). Knowledge of the unseen in its real sense is knowledge without the mediation of a physical cause. What reaches prophets through *waḥy* (revelation), the friends of Allah — the *awliyāʼ*, singular *walī*, meaning a righteous servant whom Allah has drawn near — through *ilhām* (inspiration), or diviners through their calculations and physical causes, is not that.

**The doubt, and the answer.** How, then, do we explain the reports of *awliyāʼ* who at times foretold rain, or a pregnancy, or someone's exact place of death — and were proved right? Or astrologers who occasionally hit? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers on two levels. First, what the verse denies is the *total* knowledge of these five, a knowledge comprehending everything created and every relative condition; that someone receives some partial knowledge through *ilhām* in a stray case is not contradictory to it. Second, when we say *ʿilm*, we mean absolute knowledge, and what a *walī* receives through *ilhām* is not absolute — many probabilities of error or false perception exist in it. As for astrologers and their ilk, it is a common observation that they hardly come up to the level of a single truth out of ten lies; that cannot be called absolute knowledge at all.

**A clarifying frame.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays its author's teacher, Shaykh ul-Islām Shabbīr Aḥmad ʿUthmānī, who divided *al-ghayb* into two kinds: (1) *al-aḥkām ul-ghaybiyyah*, the unseen **injunctions** — those originating from the revealed law, including knowledge of the Being and attributes of Allah (the domain of *al-ʿaqāʼid*, beliefs), and all the rulings of the Sharīʿah that tell us what meets Allah's approval and disapproval; and (2) *al-akwān ul-ghaybiyyah*, the unseen **events** occurring in the world. The first kind Allah *has* given to His prophets and messengers — *"He does not let anyone know His Unseen, except a messenger whom He chooses"* (72:26–27) — and conveying it is the very purpose of their mission. The second kind, the whole of it, is simply not given to anyone; it remains categorically exclusive to Him as His intrinsic attribute. Of it He gives partial knowledge of particular events when He wills and as much as He wills, to prophets through *waḥy* and to the *awliyāʼ* through *ilhām* — and being bestowed, it cannot in the real sense be called *ʿilm ul-ghayb*.

## Why the ayah is worded the way it is

The first three are stated **positively** (their knowledge is exclusive to Allah) and the last two **negatively** (no one other than Allah knows them). The reason: the last two are states connected with one's own person, the very ones a person might try to seek knowledge about. So for those, anyone else's access is explicitly negated. And that denial effectively proves the first three by argument: here is someone who does not know his doings and earnings tomorrow, nor the point where his life ends — how could he then be expected to know the heavens and the coming of the rains, or the thing hidden in the dark layers of a mother's womb? The first three are by themselves outside the scope of human access, so a positive statement of Allah's exclusive hold on them suffices.

Two further touches. The Hour is put in a **nominal** sentence, the rain and the wombs in **verbal** ones — perhaps, the commentary suggests, because the Last Day is a definite imperative with no change in it, while the coming of rain and the conditions of pregnancy keep changing, and a verbal sentence is suggestive of change. And with the wombs it says *"He knows"*, while with rain it says only *"He sends down"*. The point about rain is that this thing to which thousands of human benefits are tied comes at the bidding of Allah alone; that its knowledge is exclusively His already stands proved from the context.

Last, the verse says you do not know **in what land** you will die — not *when*. Why the place and not the time? Because the place of death, even if not known definitely, is something one can guess from one's outward living conditions: one naturally assumes one will die where one has settled, and at the least the place is, after all, present somewhere in the world. The time is otherwise: it lies in the future, and the future is not here yet. So if a person cannot know his place of death, despite its being actually present, how could it be imagined that he would know his time of death, which simply does not exist yet?

## Living it

Ayah 33 removes the illusion that someone else's righteousness will carry you — the most beloved person in your life cannot be your ransom, though shared faith can be the channel of benefit between you. Ayah 34 removes the illusion that you will see the deadline coming: you do not know when the Hour is, what tomorrow will bring, or the patch of earth where you will be laid down — and you may already be travelling toward it for a reason that looks entirely ordinary. What is left is *ittaqū rabbakum* — live in awe of your Lord, do not let contentment with this life lull you, do not let the deceiver talk you out of the certainty of Allah's promise. The sūrah's final words seal it: **inna Allāha ʿalīmun khabīr** — Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.
